speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As we start, Sir, I will sketch out the backdrop to the Bill, the reasons for state intervention in contracts – private contracts, we are intervening – and then I will deal with Parts 1 to 3 of this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will add that this Bill is a little bit of a Noah's Ark, because it started with Parts 1 to 3 and it took about nine days from conception to delivery.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But along the way, other Ministries have added various parts to it, so, my colleague, Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong, will deal with parts four and five, which deal with annual general meetings (AGMs) and the ability of Courts to hear matters online, virtually.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is at the request of MOF and the Supreme Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Minister Lawrence Wong will speak on property tax, which is in Part 6, and Minister Gan Kim Yong will deal with Part 7.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: MOH wanted certain orders to prevent further spread of the virus.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think Members will only be too familiar with the background – both the health situation and the economic situation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is the most serious crisis this country has faced since Independence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many around the world are describing this as the most serious crisis since the Second World War.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The human cost – in terms of deaths, infections, you look at Europe.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The economic cost all over the world – in terms of jobs; economies, devastated; peoples' lives, ruined; businesses, shuttered; investments, wiped out.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the speed at which all of this has happened, has taken many by surprise.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And at that time, there were 410,000 infections and 18,000 deaths.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Eleven days later, the situation had worsened again.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We had 1.2 million infections, more than 67,000 people dead.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is almost certainly an understatement of the true figures.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The virus is still tearing through the world.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Africa and South Asia, so far, have not been badly hit and we can only hope that it stays that way.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On 19 March, the Secretary-General of the United Nations said, a "global recession – perhaps of record dimensions – is a near certainty." On 19 March, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) made an assessment that global unemployment could increase by 25 million.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On 27 March, eight days later, ILO changed its assessment and said unemployment could be far bigger, far deeper, certainly more than 25 million.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Last week, the Director of the International Department of the People's Bank of China said, "The possibility of a 'Great Depression' cannot be ruled out if the epidemic continues to run out of control, and the deterioration of the real economy is compounded by an eruption of financial risks." The Great Depression – the phrase itself brings to mind one of the most desperate periods that America and the world went through in the 20th century.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Most of us know about the Great Depression only through books and economic studies.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The era, the mood, that desperation have been vividly captured in literature by people like John Dos Passos, Steinbeck and others.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The world has more resources, better understanding, tools, to avoid a similar Great Depression now, but the idea itself and what it can do to many people's lives is quite sobering, and the figures are grim.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the last two weeks of March, 10 million Americans filed for unemployment benefits.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In contrast during the 2008 to 2009 Global Financial Crisis, the global unemployment rose by about 22 million.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) has said that the downward pressure on foreign direct investment (FDI) could be 30 to 40% this year and next year.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Aviation has collapsed and as of 2 April, nearly 4 billion people – half of the world's population – were under some form of movement restriction.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think that does not include Singapore's figures, but that is probably a rounding error.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Spending goes down, businesses and jobs are affected, but a lot of activity continues.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Here, it is a hard stop, immediate, by government orders to most economic activity, even movement of people – overnight as it were.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the impact is that of economies literally falling off a cliff – in free fall.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is the difference between this slowdown and others.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And ours is a globalised economy and is especially hard-hit, with disruptions to the supply chain, flow of manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: External trade is three times our internal economy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And, of course, large parts of the internal economy are also being closed down.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Wide-ranging measures – job protection, immediate cash to Singaporeans, measures to help stabilise businesses, including Government-supported loans.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, on the banking and financial side, MAS has worked with the banks and announced a series of voluntary initiatives by the financial institutions – deferment of payments on mortgages; principal and interest, where the borrower wants it, can be deferred; other measures on credit flow to businesses as well.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This Bill is the third part of the response by the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And before I deal with the provisions in the Bill, there is an important point of principle that should be set out and that is this: one of the foundations for our country is rule of law and there are several key aspects to this, including sanctity of contracts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Parties are free to organise themselves, enter into whatever contracts they want as long as they are not illegal.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The general assumption is that the state will not intervene in such contracts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The reputation for upholding that is critical for Singapore as an international commercial centre with strong FDI.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, for our financial, industrial and commercial sectors, the bedrock is really our reputation for rationality in Government policy, in economic management, integrity, absence of corruption, sanctity of contracts, court system and more.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are all threaded together to form what I would call one larger golden thread.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You interfere with any of this, you risk unravelling the entire golden thread.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Yet, we are now seeking to intervene in private contracts to alter performance obligations.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will ask Members for forbearance because I will take some time on this.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is important that we understand the principles so that everyone, including investors, understand when and how we might intervene, both now and in future.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In order to look at the answers on principles of intervention, we can look at some situations when free market economies, which strongly protect the sanctity of contracts, have intervened.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Laws were passed by various American states: Iowa passed laws in 1933, 27 other states followed suit within the next 18 months.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The laws gave relief to mortgagors – a moratorium on mortgage foreclosures.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Strict enforcement of particular economic rights may not be desirable because of the damage that will cause to the whole economy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Fast forward to the Global Financial Crisis 2008/2009, laws were passed in the US to provide protection to homeowners and renters facing foreclosure.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those laws expanded the mandatory 90-day grace period to holders of all types of home loans.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Third example, after Hurricane Katrina in 2005, Mississippi implemented a moratorium that altered creditors' ability to foreclose in the two-year period after the storm.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These are just some examples, there are many others from other countries.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will summarise the principles in this way.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The starting point is sanctity of contract, agreements must be kept: fundamental, basic, underpins our economy, free market.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: People must be able to make agreements and know that they will be upheld and enforced.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That must almost be the unyielding principle and norm.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But freedom of contract is not an absolute.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, the law sets a framework, contracts are only valid if they do not breach that framework.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second, as we are seeking to do now, intervenes after the contracts have been entered into, to alter performance obligations.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For the first type of intervention, there are well-established exceptions in the law – not just in Singapore, but also in the UK, US, Australia, elsewhere for reasons of public policy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You see this in our law – Unfair Contract Terms Act, unlicensed moneylending contracts, other illegal contracts: they are not enforceable.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Courts also have the right to invalidate contracts that have been entered into in that way.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our intervention through this Bill is somewhat different.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It alters obligations under contracts which have already been formed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I gave examples from the US to this House.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I went back to take a quick look at our laws as to whether we have done something similar.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The nearest equivalent I could find is the Frustrated Contracts Act passed on 22 January 1959, which applied retroactively to all contracts if the discharge was on or after 1 January 1959.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I was actually quite surprised that the then government had the time to do this given the general situation – the Malayan Emergency and dealing with, of course, a young and irrepressible Mr Lee in Parliament in Opposition, which was probably enough to keep them occupied.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, strict enforcement of particular contractual rights could damage the whole economy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Turning then to COVID-19, the Government has had to impose border constraints, direct most businesses to shut down, get their people to work from home, and if that is not possible, no work can be done.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Imposing a whole variety of restrictions on travel and movement, these were not foreseeable.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Their impact on the supply chain – many businesses could not procure the supplies they needed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The impact on flow of manpower – sectors that depended heavily on foreign manpower like construction were seriously affected.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And according to one survey, nearly 80% will not last longer than six months, if the situation does not improve.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Severe impact as well with hotel occupancy having fallen severely.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Singapore Airlines has 96% of the fleet grounded.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In February, taxi drivers were reporting a fall in earnings of up to 30%.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In March, they were reporting a fall of up to 50% to 60%.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Meanwhile, costs continue to run, rents have to be paid.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For F&B outlets run by SMEs, rents could make up nearly 30% of their business cost and wages have to be paid as well.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The earlier survey I cited on F&B outlets suggested that 80% were planning to reduce staff to cut costs.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In this situation, we cannot say leave it to the market, leave it to the contractual situation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The bottom of the market has literally fallen off and the normal assumptions of business are gone.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Every business should plan for some severe shock, but almost none could have prepared for this and if we do not intervene, the consequences would be that those in a position of advantage will make some money but most will suffer bankruptcies, insolvencies and complete destruction of the economic arena.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Lots of grief, lots of good companies and businesses going under.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Even for those in a stronger position, many landlords do not really want to see their tenants go bust.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If I can quote Andrew Lim, CFO of Capitaland Group, "Tenants and landlords are in a long-term symbiotic relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is in our interest to see our tenants ride through this with us.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are all in this together because everyone in the eco-system has been impacted." Yesterday's Business Times had a report – “the virus is turning Europe's retail apocalypse into a nightmare for landlords and lenders".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The threat of the virus is not just to the retailers and restaurants.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The ripple effect is across real estate and banking sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Landlords will face shortfalls in income making it harder for property companies to pay interest to avoid breaching loan covenants.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And those property companies have duties to their investors which include pension funds.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As for banks, they say they are flat-out dealing with calls from existing borrowers asking for waivers.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Three packages by Deputy Prime Minister – you can compare that with the infusion of blood.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This Bill seeks to stanch the flow of blood – a reprieve for a certain period, a matter of months.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It seeks to give much-needed liquidity to commercial parties.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The immediate impact is a redistribution of monies between the parties to the affected contracts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Tenants who have to pay rentals, now they can keep the cash.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Contractors who have to pay damages, will be relieved from having to pay.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We seek to give breathing space for these businesses, to take stock, see what they can do, assess their position – with cash flow relief meanwhile.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I would call this a legal circuit breaker: a timeout until this virus dies out and contracts, like life, can return to normal.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we were to insist on the letter of the law, the last precise minutest contractual obligation, we would like Shylock, be insisting on extracting the last pound of flesh, but at the expense of the life and spirit of this country.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Better a circuit breaker, so the spirit of the law, the essence of contracts which is trust, can live and in time to come, thrive again.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I have no doubt, it will do so.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: None of us in our lifetime have encountered an economic shock like this.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the Government has to do everything to intervene to help keep some structure of the economy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not know how long this situation will last.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Thereafter, if we want to extend it, we have to come back to Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Measures under Part 2 of the Bill, they apply to obligations to be performed on or after 1 February 2020, regardless of when prior to that the contracts were entered into.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The reason we have chosen 1 February 2020 is, we believe the effects of COVID-19 began to be felt significantly in Singapore after 1 February 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Supply chains connected to events occurring outside Singapore were being disrupted.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, the measures do not apply to contracts that were entered into on or after 25 March 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On 24 March 2020, MOH enhanced the restrictions and promoted safe distancing.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, if parties, with knowledge of those facts, entered into contracts in the last few days, they should not seek help from this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If a person wants to claim relief, how does he do so?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He has got to give notice to the other party.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Once a notification has been sent, certain types of actions are prohibited.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These include: (a) commencing or continuing a legal action; (b) making an application for winding up, bankruptcy, judicial management order; (c) terminating a lease or licence of immovable property for non-payment of rent – landlords can, however, use the security deposit to offset rental payments due because that does not create additional cash flow obligation on the tenants; (d) enforcement of certain securities over immovable property.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It will also be prevented from (e) enforcement of any security over movable property used for the purpose of trade business or profession.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You cannot enforce, you cannot repossess goods used for trade business or profession.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Non-compliance is an offence punishable with a fine.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Other consequences depending on the nature of the prohibited action that is taken: action may be dismissed, voided, invalidated.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Minister will be empowered to add further categories of contracts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The reason is, as I said, we did this in nine days.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We took the contracts that we knew were clearly covered, but we wanted the ability to add in other categories should there be feedback on that.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we did not want to wait for a full assessment, allow perfection to become the opposite of what needs to be done immediately.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The first category covered leases, licences of non-residential property.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is help in real terms because the tenants will get breathing space, to adjust their businesses, survive in the medium term: it is liquidity for them.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And these measures, of course, should be seen together with other measures that the Government and the financial industry have announced.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you take an F&B outlet for example, as I said earlier, if it is an SME, nearly 30% of its business cost goes towards rental.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It will have that liquidity now in real terms and if they did not have the cash, at least they do not have to go and look for the money now.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And for those who meet the requirements under the Bill, they can then delay the payment of rent, if they wish, for some months.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In addition, of course, you have got the 75% salary support for April and the enhanced Government-supported loans at low interest and the various measures announced by MAS.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These measures do not mean that all tenants do not have to pay rent.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those who have the ability to make rental payments must continue to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Bill seeks to help those who are unable to pay and the measures are only for a period.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The landlord’s rights can be exercised after that.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, if an MNC, or a substantial company applies, it will probably not qualify because it has got to show that it is "unable" to pay, not just that business has suffered.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Two weeks ago, Germany passed emergency legislation to provide relief to individuals and businesses from the economic impact of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The German legislation provides that anyone who is affected by COVID-19 does not have to pay rent between 1 April and 30 June, and they cannot be evicted.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After the law came into force, several people said they would not be paying rent, including a string of retailers – Adidas and H&M, for example.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Adidas was reported to have made a net profit of nearly $2 billion euros last year.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: German politicians urged that financially sound companies should not take advantage of the situation and that they must show solidarity in a time of crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The officials also clarified that the law was not meant to cover entities that were able to make rental payments.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our Bill is scoped to deal with this.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some REITs, some landlords, but REITs in particular, have written to my Ministry.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are concerned that this is going to affect their returns and that the Bill is heavily weighted in favour of tenants.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: REIT Association of Singapore or REITAS has issued a public statement today, not a coincidence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They say the transfer of cash flow is a mismatch.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Deferring rental obligations transfers cash flow constraints from tenant to landlord.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They say significant strain is placed on the REIT’s ability to service its own financial and operational obligations and that the REITs have minimal financial flexibility to absorb cash flow disruption, because of the requirement to pay out 90% of income to qualify for tax exemption.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The first point is that there is a deferral of rental obligations but the rental obligations do not go away.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, the relief only applies to those who are unable to perform due to COVID.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are not going to be able to pay you anyway.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many landlords in Singapore, many others, have suffered cash flow disruptions even without the Bill; and it is not just REITs which face this.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Landlords are able to set off the security deposits they have, so, in a sense, for the first couple of months, at least, the landlords also do not have any cash flow constraints because they set off against the deposits they have.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: During that period, parties are encouraged to work out a compromise.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Assessors will try and find just and equitable outcomes, including, for example, reviewing the moratorium after three months.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, landlords also have to be realistic about the impact COVID-19 has had on the entire economy and cash flow on all sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: REITs are not the only ones affected and on the tax issues that are raised, REITAS can approach the Government and discuss precisely what the issues are.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second point that the REITAS statement makes is: the enforced interruption of revenue has the potential to degrade key metrics, in turn impacting on their financial stability.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I would say it is the pandemic and not this Bill, that has caused all these interruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Bill gives parties a better opportunity to work out a compromise quickly and without costly long-drawn litigation or legal proceedings, which will be a drag on everyone.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They also make the point that REITs are seen as a source of stable and predictable outcome and many domestic retail investors have come to reply on the regular, stable and predictable distributions that REITs provide.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So the inability of REITs to receive up to 100% of their rental income for up to six months will result in lower cash flows to REITs, who will then be compelled to lower the distributions to unitholders.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Landlords and REITs have an important, highly valuable economic function.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our task is to see how to protect as much of the business eco-system as possible – from the banks, to the landlords, to the tenants, to the consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Because the welfare of Singaporeans, their jobs, depends on the economy being protected.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we have to move quickly to give as much protection as is sensible.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have sought to explain how we have attempted to protect as much of the eco-system as possible – for individuals: cash, training grants, vouchers and more; for SMEs and tenants: there is rental protection, credit flow, mortgage protection, MAS measures, JSS.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Government is paying 75% of your employees' salaries in April and a portion of the salaries for the rest of the nine months when JSS applies, and you will also get the benefit of the credit lines and the MAS' initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The SMEs and individuals are facing a lot of pain.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If they are not helped, the entire business eco-system could crash.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Morally as well: some of this pain has to be shared.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Landlords have benefited tremendously from growth, the Government’s rational policies, good governance, low taxes in Singapore, and fairness and justice requires that they help share some of this pain, rather than leaving it to the smallest and weakest to bear it all.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If a tenant applies under the Bill, and if the landlord and tenant cannot agree, they go to the Assessors.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Assessors will see the previous year’s tax returns, the accounts; they may ask for additional information and then will determine if a tenant is unable to pay.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Generally, if a tenant is a small business and accounts show that it has been impacted by COVID-19, Assessors will likely accept that the tenant was unable to pay.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Assessors could say: suspend rental payments for three months.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Thereafter, if problems continue, come back to us.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The appeals from REITs say that they cannot evict tenants, it will affect our returns, there will be other tenants who can make up the tenancies.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If I may say so, when the whole house, meaning the whole economy, is under threat, we should try not to focus too much on our own individual rooms.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We all need to pitch in to save the economy as a whole.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I would suggest that there are broader concerns beyond the rates of return.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Is it really going to be possible for you to get the previous rates of return for the next six months?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Is it possible to have business as usual in the next few months?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if it is truly the case that the landlords can find other tenants and if the current tenant is taking advantage of the situation, let us know – that will be part of the assessment.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The landlords would benefit quite a lot, from the three packages that the Deputy Prime Minister has announced.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will make sure the Assessors are able to take all the facts into account, when deciding what is just and equitable.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second category of contracts that are covered will be construction-related contracts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The built-environment sector has felt the impact of COVID-19 and continues to feel this impact on several fronts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It started with building materials and equipment coming into Singapore from China.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Travel restrictions are likely to continue worldwide; the situation may worsen.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many construction firms will likely face financial difficulties.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The measures in this Bill will help the construction sector in the following ways.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, if a contractor is not able to perform due to a COVID-19 event between 1 February 2020 and the end of the prescribed period, that period should be disregarded in determining what is the period of delay in performance.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, the Bill provides for a defence to any claim for breach of contract.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The defence will apply if the inability occurred on or after 1 February 2020, and before the end of the prescribed period, which we will have to determine, depending on how the situation evolves.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is the size of the industry as a whole.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The third category is event and tourism-related contracts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is provided the party seeking relief has served a notification for relief on the other party.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: While many hotels and venue providers have been understanding and offered to hold on to deposits, there have been some which have simply forfeited the deposit; insisted on the event being held.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One example is a letter we received from a man who had made a booking with an event space provider.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He had arranged for his daughter’s 21st birthday celebration to be held on 4 April.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Booking had been done sometime in early March and more than 10 guests had been invited.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The man approached the event space provider to seek a refund or postponement until after the COVID-19 related measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, the spread of COVID-19 infections and the Government's control measures to address this, has meant that such meetings and Court proceedings, to be held in person or to be attended by persons physically, are no longer always possible or, even when they are, should be reduced.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On 27 March, MOH’s Safe-Distancing Regulations under the Infectious Diseases Act, came into force.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This limited gatherings outside of work and school to 10 persons or fewer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Since then, these control measures have been progressively enhanced, stepped up and made stricter.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This has given rise to some problems transacting usual commercial and other matters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many companies, including those listed on the Singapore Exchange, have been unable to hold shareholder meetings, including AGMs, to obtain shareholder approval to undertake a proposed course of action by the company.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, meetings which otherwise would be held to approve dividend payments, which can, of course, be given to shareholders and to assist in their cash flow, could not be held.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Companies could not raise capital, for example, through rights issues and share capital increases, where meetings were otherwise necessary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Since 27 March, when the Safe Distancing Regulations were stepped up and came into force, certain AGMs were also postponed as a result.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This, in turn, also meant that they would have had to defer payment of final dividends for the financial year, as these can only be approved at the AGM.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Several real estate investment trusts, such as Ascendas and OUE Commercial, have also had to defer their AGMs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And listed companies, like Capitaland and Starhub, have had to obtain extensions of time, keeping their meetings and, thereafter, their corporate plans, in abeyance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But it is not just the corporate sector which has been affected.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Similar challenges have also been faced by a range of different bodies in different sectors, for example, charities, societies, co-operative societies, trade unions and MCSTs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For these bodies, not being able to hold their meetings can have various adverse implications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some trade unions, for example, may be unable to obtain approval for additional expenditures to provide assistance to members, particularly during this COVID-19 situation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MCSTs may not be able to carry out urgent non-routine works on their estates, where subsidiary proprietors’ approvals would have been needed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: En bloc sales may not be able to complete by the stipulated timelines, if the requisite meetings are not held.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In these situations, if sellers fail to meet their deadlines, they may have to start the process all over, jeopardising existing sales arrangements and, of course, scuttling the plans of buyers and sellers alike.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Societies and charities would be unable to meet deadlines to elect officers for governance purposes, and cooperative societies unable to issue dividends to members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 27 applies to all situations where personal attendance at the meeting is provided for in written law or any legal instrument.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There need not be an explicit requirement for physical attendance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The relevant law or legal instrument may simply entitle a person to attend a meeting.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The relevant law or legal instrument may provide for both virtual meetings and personal attendance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In such a situation, clause 27 would also apply.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Compliance with the prescribed alternative arrangements will override anything to the contrary in law or the legal instrument.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The prescribed alternative arrangements are designed to be pragmatic and also practicable, given the prevailing conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Safety of the participants, in particular, will be the priority.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But there will be safeguards to facilitate informed and effective participation and, at the same time, mindful of the technological constraints and security considerations to ensure that the meeting is held regularly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The range of options that can be considered are set out in clause 27(2), which allows in appropriate cases, for meeting proceedings to take place electronically or by video-conference, or voting by electronic means or for an appropriate period of notice to be provided or enhanced, to name a few.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To illustrate, alternative arrangements for a company AGM may look something like this: the meeting can be completely virtual and there will be no need to meet physically.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Documents, such as notices of meetings or proxy forms, may be sent by electronic means, instead of hard copy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: People do not need to be in the office to do printing, copying, sealing of envelopes and so on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Notices of meetings, including electronic meetings, will have to comply with the prescribed minimum notice period, as a safeguard.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Since voting in person by everyone at the meeting is not possible, proxy voting can also be used.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As a safeguard, a specific office-holder, such as the chairman, may be designated as the sole proxy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There will also be safeguards to ensure that the meeting is conducted properly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Hence, the meeting must have “live” video and audio feed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members must be given the opportunity to submit questions, such as through email, in advance of the meeting and these questions must be addressed by the chairman or the relevant officer of the meeting before or during the meeting.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There may be some variations in the way in which these arrangements might work from one type of meeting to another; from one society to another society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Hence, under clause 27(5), the order under clause 27(1) may apply retrospectively so that any meetings held in the intervening period would be covered.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have made this known as far as possible to the market once this Bill was being prepared so that people in the market could rely on the provisions of this Bill, and know about it as soon as possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On the same day, SGX, ACRA and MAS issued their joint guidance for listed companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The guidance sets out in detail how issuers could hold meetings in compliance with the safe distancing measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Applying clause 27 retrospectively ensures that rearrangements made to meetings between 27 March and when the alternative arrangements are prescribed, will be upheld.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This includes meetings that were deferred in response to safe distancing measures, and also meetings which were reconvened after being originally deferred.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The conduct of Court proceedings in physical courtrooms will also need to be reduced during this period where control measures are in place.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Hence, more proceedings will be held remotely with the aid of technology.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Judiciary and the Syariah Court have already moved decisively prior to this in response to the measures implemented by the Government to minimise the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: During the period specified by the Judiciary and the Syariah Court, every matter fixed for hearing in the Supreme Court, State Courts and Family Justice Courts, as well as in the Syariah Court, either have already been, or will shortly be adjourned, unless assessed to be essential and urgent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Hearings during this period will, as far as possible, be conducted through electronic means.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 28 of the Bill will complement and facilitate these measures by allowing for a wider use of remote communication in Court proceedings in the following way.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 28 will allow any Court or Syariah Court proceedings to be conducted remotely, if certain conditions are met.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This means that Judges may hear the cases remotely, outside of a courtroom.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are some conditions, as I have mentioned earlier, to ensure the propriety of the proceedings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Therefore, a witness who makes an appearance or gives evidence must do so only from a place specified by the Court or the Syariah Court.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, if the witness is a witness of fact, then the parties to the proceedings must come together and agree that this witness can testify by remote communication.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Existing safeguards adapted from the Evidence Act and the Criminal Procedure Code will continue to apply.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, for example, the Court or the Syariah Court must not make an order to conduct proceedings remotely, if having regard to the overall justice of the case, the proceedings cannot be conducted fairly if proceedings were held remotely.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Fairness of the proceedings remains the overriding consideration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The existing rules which prohibit unauthorised audio or visual recordings in Court will also apply under Part 5 of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, for instance, a litigant who is engaged in remote Court proceedings cannot be recording the proceedings without the Court’s permission.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These measures, Sir, are designed to be temporary in nature and are intended to ensure the continued operation of the Courts during the COVID-19 situation as much as possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Hence, two temporal limits have been put in place.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is the period that the control measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19 are in force, or any further period necessary or expedient to conduct any proceeding in a safe and efficient manner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To help businesses affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, the Government introduced the property tax rebate for non-residential properties, as announced in the Budget and the Supplementary Budget.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The policy intent of the property tax rebate is to help the business operator affected by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Hence, the Government had strongly urged property owners to pass down the rebate to their tenants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Property owners pay property tax for each property tax account.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In many cases, one property would be covered under one property tax account.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But there are also many other cases with one property but multiple property tax accounts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, a retail mall would have multiple property tax accounts because a shop within the mall, like a retail store or restaurant, would be accounted for under a single property tax account.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government fully appreciates the property owners who have or are in the process of passing on the rebate to their tenants, either by making cash payments or by reducing rentals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In some instances, property owners have gone further to reduce rentals by an amount that is greater than the quantum of the rebate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In so doing, they have taken a step further to help their tenants and share the burden during this time of uncertainty.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: However, the Government has also received feedback, particularly from tenants, that there are property owners who have not yet passed on the rebate to them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And just to set things in perspective, a 100% property tax rebate will work out to slightly more than one month of rent for most properties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the provisions in this Bill ensure that property owners who have not passed on the rebate fully will have to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will require the property owner to pass on the rebate by making a cash payment to his tenant or by reducing or offsetting future rental payments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Property owners are also prohibited from imposing conditions when passing on the rebate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The property owner must keep records that he has so passed on the benefit and when he has done so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Failure to properly pass on the rebate or to keep a proper record is also an offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For instance, if a property tax account is for a property wholly rented out to a tenant for the whole of 2020, the property owner should pass on the full sum of the rebate he received as the rebate is entirely attributed to a rented space.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill also provides the property owner or the property owner's tenant with an avenue of redress should there be any dispute as to whether the owner has properly passed on the benefit or whether the provisions apply to the property owner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The owner or his tenant may apply to a Valuation Review Panel, which will adjudicate disputes between the owner and his tenant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Panel will then determine if the property owner has indeed passed on the rebate fully to his tenants in the required manner by the required timelines.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Panel may make further directions for compliance by the owner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A determination and any further directions of a Valuation Review Panel are appealable to the High Court if they involve questions of law, or mixed law and fact.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Further details of the pass-through of the property tax rebate to tenants will be provided under the subsidiary legislation and on the website of the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And with this Bill, we will require all property owners to do their part.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Beyond the legal requirements, we call on all stakeholders, be it landlords or tenants, to really come together in the spirit of SG United so that we can work together and overcome the impact of COVID-19 together.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This enhanced set of safe distancing measures serves as a critical circuit breaker to curb the trend of increasing local transmission of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The trend is particularly concerning in the past week.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There was also an increasing number of unlinked cases in the past week, which suggests that there are quite a number of undetected cases within our community which have led to these unlinked cases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are also starting to see the emergence of new clusters daily.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Government has taken a series of steps progressively over the last three months to curb the spread of COVID-19 in Singapore, based on our risk assessment of the evolving situation both locally and globally, as well as our anticipation of the likely trends and developments ahead of us.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It is now timely to introduce heightened measures, given the worrying trends, to curb a further rise in cases and pre-empt widespread community transmission.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In other words, we need to apply brakes, hard brakes, to slow the transmission.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is what we mean by a circuit breaker.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Enhanced safe distancing is necessary to significantly reduce movements and interactions in both public and private places.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It is an important opportunity for us to work together to slow the infection significantly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The key message is simply this: “Stay home.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: If you cannot avoid close contact, wear a mask to protect others and to protect yourself.” Everyone must play our part for the circuit breaker to be effective.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These are temporary measures specific to the COVID-19 situation we are facing currently.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Examples of essential services include healthcare, transport, cleaning services and food-related services; and supply chains, such as F&B establishments, supermarkets and food manufacturing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The list of essential services is published online (https://covid.gobusiness.gov.sg/essentialservices).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Public Service will also be fully operational and Government services will be available, but with the majority of the public service workforce telecommuting.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Services that are not essential and will therefore have to close their physical premises include fashion retail outlets, beauty and wellness services, and public and private recreational facilities, such as gyms and swimming pools, including those in private condominiums.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For premises that remain open, the Bill also provides powers to set requirements for the premises and the manner of carrying out the business while it is in operation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, F&B providers like hawker centres and restaurants can remain open but only for takeaway or delivery.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Dining-in is not allowed so as to reduce people interactions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Businesses and owners of premises that remain open will also need to implement strict safe distancing measures, such as minimising staff on-site, introducing staggered work hours or avoiding social interactions during meal times, as well as ensuring safe distancing for queues, if any.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, the Bill allows the Minister to put in place measures to restrict the movement of people in specified places, as well as to limit the usage of specific premises and facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Bill allows the Minister to restrict individuals’ movements and interactions at their place of residence or any specified place, as well as their use of common areas, such as void decks and shared facilities in HDB estates and private condominiums.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Members of the public are urged to stay at home.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There are good and necessary reasons for going out, and these will be allowed by the control order, but we would strongly urge everyone not to go out, except to purchase daily necessities, essential services, or for urgent medical needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: And when they are out, they must adhere to the safe distancing measures.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While the majority of Singaporeans are responsible and will try to comply with the safe distancing measures, there will, inevitably, be a few individuals who do not treat the situation seriously and blatantly disregard the rules.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, they may refuse to adhere to safe distancing measures put in place by F&B venues, such as coffee shops or supermarkets, or they may loiter and inter-mingle in groups in public areas instead of staying at home.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In doing so, they place themselves and others around them at risk of infection.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will not hesitate to take action against such persons and send a strong signal to prevent such behaviour from negating our collective efforts during this crucial circuit breaker to slow down the infection.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Third, the Bill also allows the Minister to prohibit events and gatherings or impose conditions on how they are conducted and on the participation in such activities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This enables us to better regulate events and gatherings, including those that take place on private properties.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This would include having private parties or gatherings with families or friends not living together, at home or in public spaces, such as in parks and HDB void decks.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Fourth, the Bill provides the option to bring the Requisition of Resources Act (RORA) into effect, for the purposes of containing COVID-19 and caring for the patients and those at risk.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This allows for the requisition of land, property or services needed to ramp up our healthcare capacity and public health capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For instance, if the number of COVID-19 cases continue to rise in Singapore, it may become necessary to requisition buildings suitable for conversion into accommodation and care facilities in order to isolate individuals who are suspected or confirmed to be infected, to reduce the risk of further spread, while caring for them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I am very grateful that, today, many hotel and building operators have voluntarily stepped forward in this difficult period to work with the Government to support the national COVID-19 efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, in a crisis like this, time is often of the essence and we cannot rely solely on commercial negotiation or the goodwill of the resource owners.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Should the RORA be invoked, the Government will exercise these provisions judiciously and work closely with the affected parties.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Bill empowers the Minister or any public officer authorised by the Minister to appoint enforcement officers to take action against individuals, business owners or entities which flout the orders and requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The enforcement officers will include police officers, public officers and health officers appointed under the Infectious Diseases Act.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For our enhanced safe distancing measures to work, we need members of the public to take the measures seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, failure to adhere to the measures without a reasonable justification will constitute an offence.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We need to send a strong signal to those who are egregious in flouting the measures, as they are putting not only themselves but also others at risk.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The penalties are aligned with those under the Infectious Diseases Act.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Apart from powers, there are also provisions in the Bill for safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, let me emphasise that the Minister may make such orders only when the Minister is satisfied that the incidence and transmission of COVID-19 constitute a serious threat to public health and that the provisions of a control order are necessary or expedient to prevent or contain the spread.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, a control order and any amendment must be presented to Parliament as soon as possible after its publication in the Gazette and Parliament may pass a resolution annulling the control order or any part of it or make any amendment of it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Third, the Minister must publish the control order such that it is brought to the notice of those affected by it, in addition to publishing it in the Gazette.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The provisions adapt existing powers on safe distancing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In addition, they allow us to close certain types of workplace premises while allowing those that are essential to everyday living and supply chains to operate.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This carefully balanced approach allows us to minimise social interactions to curb further transmission.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To consolidate and simplify the rules for all, we will be revoking the current workplace regulations and general preventative regulations once the relevant provisions have been folded into the control order made under the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will review the situation then to decide whether there is a need to extend the circuit breaker period and, if so, whether some of the measures need to be adjusted.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To sum up, Part 7 of the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Bill is needed to ensure tight adherence to the enhanced safe distancing measures in reducing the transmission of COVID-19 for the overall well-being of the nation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Everyone must play our part, act responsibly and observe the measures set out to protect our population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I ask for the support of all the Members of the House for this Bill so that, together, we can win the fight against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.10 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.47 pm until 5.10 pm.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The present COVID-19 crisis is one of epic proportions – the challenge of a generation, perhaps, several generations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The steps we take now will define how future generations of Singaporeans will view us.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For some fellow Singaporeans, this crisis could quite literally translate into a matter of life or death.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So far, we have responded robustly, firmly and decisively.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To borrow an analogy recently made by the Minister for Law, budgetary measures are the financial equivalent of an urgent blood transfusion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But he also said that just as there is a transfusion, we also need to staunch the flow of blood.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, at the outset, let me iterate my full support for the Bill while also declaring my interest as a practising lawyer.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill is exceptional, yet timely and responsive.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is exceptional because, as I understand it, the Bill was put together in a matter of days.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, the Bill acts retrospectively, something which lawyers normally discourage, given that it departs from one of the main principles underlining the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nevertheless, in my view, this is well justified under these extenuating circumstances.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is also timely and responsive for several key reasons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, the Bill offers much needed reprieve – reprieve in the form of certainty that there is a window to breathe such that there is a hope that businesses can be resuscitated when the situation improves.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Collectively, they provide a sturdy mast in choppy waters.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For many of our businesses, the global economic repercussions of COVID-19 and our local circuit breaker measures mean revenues have dwindled to nearly nothing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While these economic circumstances are not due to their own actions, the impact means that businesses essentially have multiple swords hanging over their heads.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If these liabilities are allowed to vest and fall due, businesses would be starved of their cash flow and would very possibly be forced out of business.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It means that when the global situation gets better, we would have few businesses left standing to ride the wave of recovery.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need businesses to stand, and this Bill helps us do that.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For event and tourism-related contracts, additional reprieve is provided in clause 7.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many of these contracts involve the placement of deposits, which do not involve small sums of money.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 7(2) ensures that these deposits cannot be automatically forfeited, thus allowing contracting parties to look for an alternative arrangement without the fear of financial loss.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It may seem like a small measure but for man individuals and beleaguered small and medium-sized businesses that have paid deposits, I believe this will go a long way in alleviating a significant portion of their cash flow concerns.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, this Bill allows for a situation of a reduced threat of litigation, insolvency, bankruptcy, landlord-tenant disputes, hire purchase disputes from hanging over struggling businesses over the course of the next few months.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This can be seen in part three of the Bill, which modifies various Acts to give temporary relief to financially distressed individuals and businesses.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These significant changes will allow management teams to channel their mental energy towards keeping their businesses afloat and viable post-crisis, rather than or instead of them having to think about how to fend off litigation and insolvency actions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Essentially, this Bill allows management to use their mental energy to innovate, ride the storm and survive post-crisis, rather than to having to stave off and fend off insolvency proceedings or bankruptcy proceedings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I think it is a much needed reprieve.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, Sir, I seek a number of clarifications on the status of legal action and cases already commenced before the Bill comes into force.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, I am in particular talking about hire purchase vehicles and landlord-tenant disputes – cases and actions arising around those areas.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, the Bill sets out amendments to facilitate the conduct of court proceedings using remote communications technology.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nevertheless, Mr Deputy Speaker, I wish to clarify a few points about the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, the Bill provides a mechanism to manage disputes arising from the application of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Division four of part two of the Bill contains provisions relating to the appointment of Assessors, the means for applying for an assessment, the powers of an Assessor, as well as provisions relating to costs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is no good for anybody if these Assessors are stretched so thin that they are under immense time pressure to assess their cases.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have a further query on clause 13.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This flexibility may allow for a more just and equitable finding or assessment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, in situations where private landlords themselves do not have deep pockets and need the rent to pay toward a mortgage payment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By this, I mean private landlords who are landlords of commercial premises and they are unable to service their mortgage.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will some flexibility also be accorded to them in the assessment process.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, a key point about the Bill is that it merely suspends obligations but does not negate their need to be fulfilled.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In short, the Bill is like a dam, which holds back the tide of obligations temporarily.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Notwithstanding my questions and suggestions, I stand in support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fundamentally, it is about helping enterprises during this difficult period by addressing their cash flow concerns and freeing them up to think about how to survive and innovate through this crisis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is a comprehensive and significant Bill and I wish to applaud the Ministry of Law, AGC, relevant public agencies and those consulted during its drafting for investing such an immense amount of effort in such a short amount of time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It really does show the efficiency of our legal partners and the legal system at play in these extenuating circumstances.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am confident that by passing this Bill, this House would be taking a significant step in ensuring that businesses in Singapore have a much better shot of making it through the crisis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And for that reason, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A few months ago, no one could have imagined the disruptions on personal lives and businesses that we are witnessing due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: From personal celebrations or significant events to commercial contracts and commitments, the inability to proceed with plans has had both economic, social and personal consequences.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Weddings and festivities have to be postponed indefinitely, tours, vacations and major business events deferred.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Businesses have not been able to perform or deliver on their commitments due to factors beyond their control with measures taken by governments around the world, including Singapore, to stem the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As the Minister has said in his speech, the measures, though temporary, are substantial and significant.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Bill seeks to provide temporary relief to individuals and businesses who are unable to fulfill their contractual obligations because of the impact of COVID-19 and related public health measures, which no one could have foreseen or imagined.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Bill seeks to provide protection for bookings from forfeiture of deposits.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is fair for businesses as they have collected the deposits and the bookings will still be honoured and event held, albeit when it is feasible to do so.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is already distressing and disappointing for couples to have to postpone their wedding celebrations or individuals having to reschedule significant events for circumstances that are beyond their control.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The cost for such events is not small and deposits paid are also not trivial.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The same applies for tours or travel that have been paid for.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With border controls and traffic restrictions imposed to prevent the spread of COVID-19, it is therefore fair that there should be protection from forfeiture of deposits or payments made in such circumstances while maintaining the sanctity of the contract.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I understand and agree that tenants may need relief to minimise impact on their business cash flow due to the severe fall in demand on their business due to COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will allow businesses to continue to pay expenses to allow them to operate and most importantly, to keep jobs and to pay their workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, on the flipside, the landlord too will be impacted by the delay in payment of rent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Could the Minister share if there will be relief provided for landlords who, due to the inability to collect rent from tenants in such circumstances, are themselves impacted materially and therefore unable to fulfill their other contractual obligations due to the dependency on rental payments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Will there be temporary relief for them as well?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
