text: The rental arrears, even if no interest is charged, will not be a small sum.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And here, I do have some concerns, because what it means is that the tenants will end up accumulating outstanding rental debt, which still needs to be paid after the relief period.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As the Minister had mentioned in his speech, rent is not an insignificant proportion of the cost that businesses are paying.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, there will still be a large sum that tenants will have to pay after this period.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Even if the businesses were viable before the impact of COVID, as the COVID situation improves, business will pick up, but it will take some time to rebuild and it would not be easy for the individual or industrial tenants to be able to settle the outstanding rental immediately.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Would it not be better for the Assessor, while still allowing for temporary relief, to determine whether to allow tenants and landlords to renegotiate the terms of the contract that would be more viable and equitable for both parties.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will not only provide temporary relief for tenants but also minimise a situation where the debt accumulated after the relief period is too large to be repaid.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If the debt is too large, the landlord may then also be left with the short end of the deal even after having not received rent during the relief period.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am glad to hear that Minister had indicated that the Assessor will review the moratorium after three months of the relief.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So that I hope will also allow them to calibrate the impact of the debt and may be make an assessment at that point in time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the same way that the Bill sets out to give temporary relief to the tenants, the Bill also seeks temporary relief and protection for contractors from non-performance of contractual obligation caused by COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A contractor’s delay of works or a non-performance for supply of goods, even if it is due to the unexpected consequences of a COVID-19 event will adversely impact individuals or businesses that the works or supply was committed for.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Could Minister also share on how individuals and businesses impacted in such circumstances or such situations be supported?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are seeing appeals for renovations works impacted with the latest announcement of the circuit breaker measures that come into effect today.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This may result in renovations works for the flat that the seller is moving to would not be able to be completed in time and this may leave the seller with no plans to move to when they are required to hand over the current flat.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If they do ask for temporary relief of their contractual obligations to the buyer of the flat, this could create a chain effect.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If my interpretation of the Bill is correct, a practical approach for all parties would be to apply for the temporary relief during the circuit breaker period and this would then allow everyone to take the pause without having material impact on all parties involved.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am not sure whether that is the right interpretation but, basically, it would then allow everyone to not have to be impacted if there are delays.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The last point that I like to touch on is the temporary measures concerning the remission of property tax.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Clauses 30 and 31 of the Bill provide the avenue for the tenants to take action against the landlords for failing to do so and how and when it can be enforced.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is therefore necessary for these significant measures proposed in the Bill to provide temporary relief for individuals and businesses affected by COVID-19 who are unable to perform their contractual obligations while still upholding the right to exercise contractual obligations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The essence of this Bill that Minister has stressed is that everyone needs to come together to take our collective approach and I agree with him on this, the spirit of this approach because given what we are seeing in the impact of COVID-19 on everyone, unless we take a collective approach, it is going to be quite difficult for us to move forward effectively.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: MinLaw further explained that: “The COVID-19 pandemic, and associated public health measures imposed by governments around the world, has had unprecedented and unforeseeable social and economic impact.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are supply chain disruptions and manpower shortages, among other consequences.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In many cases, this has undermined the ability of individuals and businesses to fulfil contractual obligations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It would thus be unfair to hold them strictly liable for their failure to do so.” Minister Shanmugam had also given a more elaborate explanation for the basis of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It provides some form of temporary relief to people or businesses who are adversely affected by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, there are a few areas which I hope that the Minister can provide some clarification and perhaps the thinking behind the Bill.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: First, relief against termination of lease for non-residential property.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They feel that this suspension of their rights under the tenancy agreement would affect their cash flow negatively.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The landlords worry that they would have to pay hefty interest or late charges on their loans with their financiers when they cannot collect the rent from the tenant.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They also worry that the tenant may after six months, become insolvent, then they, the landlord be left without legal recourse except against the security deposit paid by the tenant.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, it seems that if the tenant does not pay the rental arrears in full after the six months, the landlords are at greater risk because the Bill exposes them to an eventual law suit by the bank.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The bank can go after the landlord, go after the security and they can repossess the property but the landlord cannot claim against the tenant if the tenant becomes insolvent.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The other concern which I have is how does the law ensure that tenants understand that this Bill merely provides the tenant temporary relief from certain legal action?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: At the end of six months, the tenant would still have to pay the arrears of rental plus applicable interest under the tenancy agreement.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But if the tenant is struggling to pay the entire rental for a few months, how realistic is it to expect that the tenant can suddenly at the end of six months magically cough up the entire six months arrears of rental.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Will this Bill give struggling tenants a false sense that they can escape their legal obligations?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, I have residents who say that they are unable to shift out from their tenanted residential homes because their contractors cannot complete the renovations of the home due to the suspension of activities or the circuit breaker order imposed by the Government.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can a tenant of a residential home in this case seek relief under this Bill?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Clause 7 of the Bill provides that if an event, for example a wedding or a tourism-related contract, is unable to proceed due to a COVID-19 related event, then the venue provider cannot forfeit the person’s deposit unless the provider obtains a determination from an Assessor that it would be just and equitable to forfeit the whole deposit or a part thereof.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, the suspension of the rights against forfeiture is for a period of only six months.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: According to the press, some couples have stated that they are unable to postpone their wedding to another date within the next six months.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There is no certainty whether the COVID-19 situation can be resolved by then and whether their wedding can then proceed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The organisation of a wedding or for that matter, a convention, a conference, a concert or a sports event takes many months of planning.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This current situation leaves too much uncertainty for all parties.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are guest lists to plan and logistics arrangements to be made.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would it not be better to allow the contracting party to cancel the contract and to just pay for whatever reasonable expenses incurred to date by the venue provider?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would there be a similar prohibition against forfeiture of deposits paid.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can the consumer who booked the tour or the air ticket be allowed to claim relief from forfeiture?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Bill provides for the appointment of Assessors by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Under clause 13 of the Bill, the Assessor’s determination is binding on all the parties to the application.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There is no appeal from an Assessor’s determination.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These are very wide and discretionary powers given to the Assessors.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Lawyers are specifically excluded from the hearing by the Assessors.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How does MinLaw ensure that the appointed Assessor will always be impartial and make a determination or adjudicates in a fair and equitable manner?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I think this is far better than moral suasion which the Government has been asking the landlords to act upon.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: To all the landlords who had already planned to pass on the tax remission to the tenants, my heartfelt thanks for doing your part in helping your tenants survive this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, my thanks to the Minister for making this happen.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, the Singapore Government has introduced stricter measures including safe distancing; restrictions on inbound visitors and putting in place a circuit breaker to pre-empt escalating coronavirus infections.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: All these calibrated and necessary measures have a direct impact not only on industries that rely on tourists such as hospitality, leisure, food and retail services, but also their ancillary industries such as landscape, cleaning and security that support such affected industries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Now, we are beginning to see the effect beginning to creep to many other sectors as well.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of these industries also employ Malaysian workers to supplement their local workforce.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That said, some companies in such ancillary industries like cleaning and environmental services companies, landscape firms and security agencies are caught off-guard by the sudden announcement and had little time to react.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, it is understandable that many of them may not be able to meet their contractual obligations during this period if their Malaysian workers do not opt to stay in the accommodations provided by the companies or choose to be with their own families across the causeway.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Security Industry Council, made up of the union for security employees and the two security associations, issued an appeal to the service buyers of security services urging them "to be reasonable and flexible as regards to the security agencies' contractual obligations, including the imposition of liquidated damages, during this exceptional period".

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Similar appeals were made by the Tripartite Committees for the environmental services and landscape industries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Avoid unnecessary punitive actions because the situation was brought about by circumstances beyond their control.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the support of our Government, many of these companies are doing their best to help their affected workers, while continuing to provide the essential services to the best of their abilities.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This brings me to my second point – due to reduced traffic from customers resulting in a significant drop in revenue, some establishments have requested for reduction in contract fees from their service providers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While it is understandable that service buyers who are affected by the COVID-19 situation are finding ways to cut costs, I hope this Bill will compel service buyers to work with their service providers and work out a win-win solution for both parties.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should they wish to scale down the essential services and contract fees, they should be pragmatic, fair and understand that it would mean a reduction in service frequency or standards.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While service providers would like to help their clients manage their cost, they also hope that the service buyers give them ample time to do the necessary adjustment.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In another case, a well-known landscape company had been given a stop work order for the maintenance of plants by some of their commercial clients during the circuit breaker period.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: No service payment will be made during this period.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such cases are faced by many service providers of essential services.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These companies are trying very hard to redeploy their workers but, it has not been easy.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite the cleaners or security officers having to work extra hard, these service buyers want to squeeze their service providers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The wage subsidy is meant to relieve financial pressures on companies as they weather the storm; and not be used as a lever for anti-competitive practice.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The reality is that it can be difficult for the management of the service providers to voice their objection for fear of having their contract terminated or be in a less favourable position during contract renewal in future but, neither do they have the finances to pay for the workers under their employment if there is no payment of contract fees.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):  : The COVID-19 pandemic has caused major disruption to businesses and workers' livelihoods in an unprecedented way and with much uncertainty when this crisis will end.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The sudden announcement by the Malaysian government imposing a Movement Control Order has affected many companies in Singapore that rely on them as part of their workforce.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, the Singapore Government has introduced stricter measures to contain the spread of the virus, including social distancing, closing borders to inbound visitors and implementing the circuit breaker from today.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I hope this bill will stop service buyers from imposing any liquidated damages for any shortfall in service standards or a reduction of manpower of manpower at the work site.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe it would be our spirit of solidarity peppered with a lot of empathy and compassion that will pull us through this crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, this Bill specifically helps those who may be unable to meet their contractual obligations due to COVID-19 as well as the related public health measures imposed in Singapore and around the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This legislative measure not only helps provide temporary cash-flow relief to businesses and individuals, it also avoids the problematic situations of damages claims, forfeiture of deposits, costly litigation actions, premature insolvency proceeding, termination of leases; among others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this very difficult time, the last thing we want is to be embroiled in legal tussles.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the stepped-up circuit breaker measures being introduced this week and further impact to businesses, these relief measures would now be even more needed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In many other jurisdictions such as US, UK, Australia and Germany, similar temporary measures have also been implemented in various forms due to COVID-19; such as moratorium on evictions, quasi force majeure.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In some jurisdictions, it is by way of Executive Order.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The key word in this Bill is that the protection and relief from legal actions in those areas prescribed are temporary in nature.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We still want to uphold the sanctity of contracts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Minister has also emphasised in the Second Reading speech that the new laws do not absolve or remove contractual obligations but merely suspend them for a prescribed period so that more time can be given to both contracting parties to work on a resolution.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While clause 5(3) of the Act set out the list of prohibited actions, can I ask the Minister if the Act also prohibit the other party from imposing interest or late penalty fee for non-payment of rents during this relief period?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Parties are also not allowed to engage lawyers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are a very important neutral party and have the final say in their ruling.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given the powers accorded by this Law, can I ask the Minister who are these Assessors and what are their credentials?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Everyone is impacted by COVID-19 one way or another.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, when the rental arrears begin to pile up, the risk of a bigger rental default by the party seeking the relief would also increase six months down the road.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our economic agencies like ESG may need to consider other assistance measures to help some of these companies including providing financing support schemes for a longer instalment repayment plan, for example.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope that most hotels would agree to the change of dates when requested; even if they have not done it on a goodwill basis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I met a constituent at my Meet-the-People Session last week, who runs an event company.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He said that such relief measures would actually put his company and him in a difficult spot.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since the COVID-19 outbreak, there were a number of cancellations of events and he still have his overheads to cover.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The deposits that he collected are actually meant to be sort of his safety net but he now may not have them anymore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have advised him to apply for the Self-Employed Person Income Relief Scheme although he said while he is grateful to the Government for this Scheme is helpful is unlikely to get him out of the dire state.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One concern I have is whether this non-forfeiture of deposit will lead to counter actions where service provider now may insist on an upfront payment or price the risk of non-forfeiture of deposit in the fees that they charged.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, we have to be mindful of such counter actions when they come.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The various public health measures, border controls, shortage of manpower and supplies can all lead to delays and cost overruns in construction projects.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If these delays resulted in hefty penalties, it could put contractors in a tenuous position.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Singapore, due to the intense competition in this sector and the tender system, the terms of most construction contracts tend to favour the developers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Most contracts do not have specific clauses that clearly allow a contractor to seek relief.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Whether the impact and disruption from COVID-19 constitute a force majeure situation actually remains to be tested and established.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, this Bill which provides reliefs from liability of non-performance is most in need under current circumstances to help especially the smaller construction companies cope with the crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Trying to keep up with the servicing of the loans and hire-purchase by banks and finance companies is another stress point companies and self-employed person faced during this period.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, I declare my interest that I work in a financial institution.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Kudos to MinLaw, MTI, MOF and the relevant stakeholders for turning this Bill around in such a short time.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the latest circuit breaker measures, their businesses will be hit even harder.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A few days ago, a Straits Times article reported on how severely retailers in our heartland malls, such as JCube in Jurong East, Lot One in Choa Chu Kang and the Star Vista in Buona Vista have been hit.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These shops tend to rely heavily on in-store sales for their revenues and the recent movement restrictions therefore have a heavy impact.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All these business declines have a domino effect and multiplier impact through our entire eco-system.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When the revenues for these businesses dry up, their employees' wages dwindle, reducing their ability to spend on goods and services and thus, in turn, affecting other businesses as well.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Landlords would have trouble collecting rentals and consequently, their lenders and investors like banks, finance companies, corporations, shareholders and other individuals would end up with non-performing loans and investments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must continue to support them as they will be the future drivers of our growth, especially if they are able to exploit regional and international opportunities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: COVID-19 is an unprecedented crisis for our generation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Without sufficient support, many otherwise flourishing businesses with good foundations might go bust and this will hamper the growth of our economy as a whole.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I strongly believe that we will all recover from this pandemic.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When the crisis is over, it will be a different world and we have to be ready to seize the new opportunities on the horizon.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We cannot afford to have a large number of small business owners being embroiled in litigation and insolvency proceedings.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They will become a drag on our economic recovery.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This Bill will give SMEs the breathing room to examine the way they do business and revamp.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They will not need to worry about fire-fighting and their immediate future.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hopefully, the temporary measures will provide them a reprieve, giving them the space and energy to review how they could change their business models and emerge from the crisis stronger.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also hope that the bigger players – landlords, banks and finance companies – will continue to see their relationships with SMEs as one of partnership.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When the SMEs do well, they will also do well.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that this understanding will underpin the future discussions that are needed between landlords and tenants, banks and borrowers, to chart a way forward.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have interests too in businesses that are tenants in malls.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During these very difficult times, the Government has rolled out a suite of measures to minimise the financial impact of COVID-19 on individuals and businesses.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand and support the intention of these measures, which aim to mitigate the financial stress experienced by businesses, big and small.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I fully support the proposed legislation to ensure that landlords pass down the property tax rebates fully to tenants.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a move in the right direction and in line with the spirit of collective responsibility to overcome COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Understandably, rentals and wages are two of the more significant costs of running an enterprise.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In effect, landlords can demand immediate repayment upon the expiry of the rent deferment period.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Businesses would not have improved multiple folds to enable the tenants to pay the arrears immediately.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill should also give guidance on leases with expiry dates that fall within the deferment period.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The rent deferment measures will provide temporary but essential relief for many businesses.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For those which are healthy and viable, the measures will provide a reprieve against the sudden impact of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ideally, they should take this opportunity to urgently restructure and update their operations and business models to become more effective and productive.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My concern is that the temporary rent deferment measures may inadvertently result in some companies over rely on a short-term relief and neglect taking the painful but necessary steps to revamp their operations.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such companies may instead hope for an upturn and postpone figuring out their next move to only six months later.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some businesses were in fact, already unviable before the onset of COVID-19, and had been having difficulties paying their rent.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, this measure merely serves to prolong the last breaths of untenable businesses.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The cumulative costs of their final months will end up being passed to their landlords.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Lease termination for such unviable tenants will release the affected properties back into the market for other businesses that may want to take advantage of the weaker rental market to set up shop.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a more organic and sustainable model for the real estate industry.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should not impede the emergence of new start-ups with potential.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As it is, this Bill creates significant uncertainty for landlords.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe that for landlords to be constructive in their assistance to tenants, landlords need to have clarity of their cash flow and strength of their balance sheet.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Rather than working out how to address delays in or non-payment of rent which affect their ability to service mortgage payments, they can plan additional relief for tenants with greater confidence in their financial position.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will be of tangible help to viable businesses.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Heng cited in his speech, there are landlords who have given additional rental assistance over and above the property tax rebates to tenants.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is important to recognise the mismatch in the obligations of tenants and property owners.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The landlord's collateral with the bank is the property whereas the tenant's lease collateral is a security deposit of between one and four months.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This security deposit is insufficient to ensure that the tenants pay after the six-month rent deferment period, which may be extended to a year.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the worst-case scenario, when the tenants go bust after six months, there is little that the landlords can do to recover their outstanding debts.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In reality, landlords have little legal recourse when a private limited company goes belly-up.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In short, the landlord will be left holding on to the bad debt.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Smaller landlords who have less resources, including individuals who own shops or strata titled offices, would face challenges meeting their obligations to their banks.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At this point, we do not know how many companies will take up the option to defer their lease payments for six months.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Rental income is the landlord's main source of cash flow to pay for mortgages and interest.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, if many companies do take up this option, there are significant implications for our banking and financial system.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This may result in landlords breaching covenants, such as interest cover ratio, related to bank loans and other debt instruments, which would result in an event of default where loans will be immediately due.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Landlords will also have no further access to credit lines to meet their operational needs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While this Bill provides temporary relief to SMEs, this relief is not extended to larger landlords who face the same issue of covenant breach and loans being called by the banks.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As responsible enterprises, landlords would go into a cash preservation and survival mode, with cuts in maintenance expenses, wages and reduce distribution to investors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: S-REITs, as institutional landlords and which represent a cornerstone of the Singapore investment landscape would be in a similar situation of financial stress.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are basically holding back cash in anticipation of worse situation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They have come to depend on S-REIT distributions to supplement their retirement and household income.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The impact of this Bill will cascade down to individual retail investors, who in turn are also consumers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This could lead to sentiments of increased pessimism and caution, dampening domestic consumption and spending and result in even less business for the tenants which the Bill intends to assist.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Plenty has been said and done about help for the vulnerable and low-income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With this Bill, our middle income Singaporeans and above may find some relief as well as employees who are working for them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Among them are entrepreneurs, small-time business owners, SMEs and sole proprietors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of them have to sustain financial obligations, but fear that they may possibly have to fold their businesses or declare bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These measures will go a long way in helping to tide them over and keep them afloat during these tough times.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, this Bill and its enforcement only allows temporary relief from the effects of COVID-19 while still upholding the right to exercise contractual obligations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the issue of fairness, my speech largely touches on how this bill would help the tenants and customers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, at the onset I would like to also mention that the other side of the contract – the landlords and the other party in the contractual obligation should also be taken into consideration.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, the impact on the landlords, for example, in the case of real estate investment trusts or REITs, may also have an impact on retail investors invested in these REITs and thus, Singaporeans will have some exposure in the eventuality that the tenants are not able to pay the rent at the end of the six months or duration stipulated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The negative feedback loop is something to take into consideration for both sides of the contractual obligation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   Among those undeniably affected are young couples who are looking forward to their wedding and starting a new life together this year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what should have been a happy event has turned into a stressful and worrying time, because they are scrambling to contact various service providers to discuss the fate of their down payments or instalments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will they be protected if they cancel their bookings for their big event?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are the deposits protected under the new legislation only relate to hotel bookings or does it include event companies that are organizing the ceremony?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How about companies that provide floral arrangements, bridal cars, videography and photography services?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The deposits have been paid but the event will not take place.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can these contractors or companies insist that the contract must be postponed to another date and cannot be cancelled?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have spoken to some young couples who voiced their concern about this situation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Unsurprisingly, some of them saved a huge amount of money for their wedding only to realize, after all that, financial prudence is key.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, for those considering postponement, the venue owners are unable to provide any date for their premises to re-open, and therefore it is difficult to come to any agreement with the other service providers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, some couples hope to get back their deposits, but these requests has been rejected.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They were instead asked to convert their payment into credit for other events or even look for another couple to take over their wedding package.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, moving forward, this Bill will hopefully provide some financial help for them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English) Mr Deputy Speaker, I would also like to ask about events slated in the later part of the year, particularly in the year end.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are always plenty of events in the festive period.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Most of them are regular annual offerings, whether it is for Christmas, for travel, for the school holidays, and so on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is it wise to start committing resources to future events or should everyone put all plans on hold until there is significant improvement in the virus situation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would it be responsible of service providers, for example, an event venue, to market their services and accept deposits without clear knowledge of whether it would be legal to host the event on the stipulated date?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Government consider protection to contracts for such events, especially those that are being held annually?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even before stricter measures were imposed, many businesses and individuals had voluntarily cancelled or postponed the events at the expense of their own pockets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some couples were about to cancel their wedding venue bookings and opted for a smaller venue for more intimate gathering or even tapped on live streaming.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some events do cancel their bookings of physical space in favour of a digital or virtual concept.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I wonder if the Government will consider making some concessions for them, should they make an appeal.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: After all, they opted for the difficult choice of cancellation out of goodwill for the fellow Singaporeans when postponement was not an option before this Bill came out.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How many disputed contracts does the body of Assessors expect to see to and how long would applicants have to wait for their turn?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there any other qualifying factors such as the scale of the event and contracted amount involved?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will their inability to fulfill contractual obligations count against their credit ratings and future ability to take on other contracts, in particular for SMEs?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is necessary because there has been feedback about landlords not doing so and many Members of the House have mentioned this earlier.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The benefit may be passed on a single method or combination of methods, including but not limited to payment of money by lump sum or way of instalments or an offset against rent or licence fee payable by tenant.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For payments and other methods, what sort of documentation will suffice as a form of reference and evidence within this Bill?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would it have to be a formal contract or would a payslip do?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What also is the longest period of instalment that can be made?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, section 29 states that IRAS gives property tax remission to certain landlords.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It also obliges those landlords to pass on the benefit of remission to tenants.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So if a landlord fails to do this, it is an offence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, we can have a situation where in early March, a landlord, out of sympathy for its tenants, reduces their rent, say, by 30%.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The landlord will get his property tax remission but he must pass it on to his standards.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, his tenants get double benefit and the landlord, having acted generously earlier, gets none.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The question is, must this landlord still pass the benefit of the property tax remission to his tenants – section 29 states he must – or is this something which he can dispute under section 30 of the Bill?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My next point is on the bankruptcy limits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, individuals and businesses must be reminded that the section 5 temporary relief is only a moratorium.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: After the prescribed period, the whole sum that was unpaid will become due.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think we need to reiterate this point to those that are utilising this deferment period within this Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Businesses should use the prescribed time to work out longer-term adjustments with their landlords.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Otherwise, they may face the risk of ballooning debt once the prescribed period is over.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Businesses should utilise all other assistance – salary subsidies that have been given out in the Budget, but this moratorium would be a meaningful supplement, nonetheless.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In concluding, I wish to take this opportunity to call for more support and empathy for the middle-income Singaporeans and also Permanent Residents or PRs, who have contributed significantly to our national reserves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If there will be a further package or new relief schemes, please let them be eligible for more help.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some are still reeling from the effects of a weakened economy previously and now, with COVID-19, there are people who have been jobless or intermittently jobless for more than a year while struggling to sustain financial and family obligations on their savings.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that there is always help available to those in need on a case-by-case basis but they should not be made to go through a significant amount of red tape to receive it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Unity, Solidarity and Resilience Budget that has been released by Deputy Prime Minister Heng today actually shows a wide range of help for various groups.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I think over time, if the virus outbreak worsens, they are definitely going to need help.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a grave time for everyone, but the Bill addresses many pressing concerns and will restore some confidence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The number of COVID-19 cases worldwide has exceeded a million.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the fight continues to limit the number of cases, it is important that the economic and practical impacts of the pandemic be addressed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This current Bill drafted under considerable pressure and sought to be passed on an expedited basis goes a long way towards addressing that.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have five points to make on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the deferment period for the rent repayment for commercial tenants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: People support this but hope that additional measures will be introduced.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While this is intended to create some breathing space for commercial tenants, rent will still accrue and will be payable at the end of the six-month period.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many are appreciative that we are proposing this but some do not feel much relief from this protection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One of my residents who is a shop owner shared her concerns with me.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She told me that she might as well wind up her business now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to remember that not only do tenants face the very real risk or possibility of winding up, landlords also faced significant risks if tenants are unable to pay at the end of six months and have no choice but to wind up.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Straits times has already reported that retail sales have dipped by up to 8.6% in February alone, at the start of this crisis, before further measures have been taken.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With the circuit breaker measures requiring all non-essential businesses to stop operations, commercial tenants are likely to be hit harder than ever.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Minister Vivian noted in his media interview, Singapore took four months to pass the SARS outbreak and six months to recover from its economic impact.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He then said that, "This problem and its aftermath, the economic aftermath, is going to last at least a year".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our relief efforts need to take into account the reality that it will not be business as usual after six months.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Minister consider an extended period for repayment of rent accrued in these six months?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can we allow tenants to repay this outstanding amount via monthly instalments spread out over a period of time?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would increase the chances of repayment to landlords and of businesses surviving.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The German government similarly passed a Bill to mitigate the consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Tenants will have until 30 June 2022 to pay back the rental arrears accrued during this period.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can we consider a similar measure in Singapore, which would benefit both landlords and tenants?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification relates to the transfer of benefit of property tax remittance from landlords to tenants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Clause 29(1) requires a landlord to pass the benefit of any profit tax remission related to COVID-19 on to the tenant.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not clear from the Bill that tenants will be required to pass on this property tax remissions to sub-tenants and sub-licensees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A significant group that may fall through this gap is users of co-working spaces that lease or licence the space from co-working companies as sub-tenants and sub-licensees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Business Times reported in September 2019 that co-working spaces take up 3.7 million square feet of Singapore's commercial space and it is one of the top six occupier sectors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify whether the benefits from property tax remissions will have to be passed on to sub-tenants and sub-licensees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is a recommendation to alleviate the rental burden on tenants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While larger landlords like CapitaLand and Mapletree have announced rent alleviation for their tenants, many other landlords have not.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the economic impact proves to be extremely dire and further remedial measures are needed, will the Minister consider looking into mandating a degree or rent abatement for the tenants?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that landlords are not exempt from the effects of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, some are more financially capable of weathering the crisis than others, and measures are required to ensure that economic impact is equally distributed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Rent abatement measures, if necessary, can be calibrated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It can be targeted at larger landlords who are in a better position to shoulder some of the economic losses and smaller tenants who have greater need for such relief.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My fourth point relates to assistance to freelancers from contractual obligation, in particular, obligations under long-term vehicle leases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Clause 5 of the Bill will help individuals who are unable to meet their obligation under a hire purchase agreement for commercial vehicles for the prescribed period of six months.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Commercial vehicles are defined under the Schedule of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the definition of commercial vehicles does not appear to extend to freelancers, such as property and insurance agents, who leased their vehicles for business-related activities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This concern was raised to me by a resident who is a property consultant who uses a car for property viewing and business-related activities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her business has been affected by the pandemic but it is not feasible for her to cancel her long-term lease as she would need the car to recover from this downturn.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She has requested that the vehicle leasing company defer her monthly lease payments for a few months until her cash flow has stabilised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, she was informed by the company that as the Government did not announce any measures relating to vehicle leases for freelancers like herself, the company did not know how to help her and was not obliged to do so either.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Freelancers like this resident need all the help they can get right now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final clarification has to do with factual witnesses giving evidence through remote communication technology in Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In contrast, consent of parties is not a prerequisite for expert witnesses to give evidence through remote communication technology under 28(2)(b)(i).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I can appreciate that a possible reason is that it is more important for the Court to be able to see the body language of factual witnesses in person as opposed to independent expert witnesses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Body language may not come across fully through remote communication technology.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Having said that, there are a number of cases that would involve overseas witnesses and there is no telling how long border restrictions will be in place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lawyers have expressed to me the concern that trial timelines will be unnecessarily prolonged and the backlog of cases may result if parties unreasonably withhold consent to the use of remote communication technology for factual witnesses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I like to thank the Government for all its efforts and hope my recommendations can be considered.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I join hon Members who spoke before me to commend officers from MinLaw, MND, MOH, the Attorney-General's Chambers and top practitioners from private practice for working together and coming up with this Bill so quickly in nine days.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is an excellent example of the spirit of SG United in action.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As mentioned by the hon Minister for Law, the introduction of this Bill on a Certificate of Urgency is precipitated by the most serious crisis our country has faced since Independence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is worth repeating that the focus of this Bill is to ensure the economic survival of contracting parties affected by the COVID-19 event, particularly the individuals and small-and-medium enterprises.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I agree, therefore, that the current circumstances are exceptional to justify intervention into the hallowed principle of sanctity of private contracts and the rule against retrospective application of laws.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister shared a precedent in the form of the Frustrated Contracts Act which was put into effect in February 1959 but applied to all contracts, even those entered into before the commencement date of the statute.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Coincidentally, the subject matter of the Frustrated Contracts Act also deals with intervening unanticipated events affecting contractual obligations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To make up, I will end with the suggestion application on what could, perhaps, be considered in future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I agree with the drafting approach in this Bill of providing relief to scheduled contracts described in the schedule.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The other option would be to just have provisions of general application.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am glad to note that, under clause 18 of the Bill, it is proposed that the Minister be given powers to amend or add to the schedule.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the uncertainties we face, this makes eminent sense.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, the wording in clause 5(1)(a) of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is one of the primary triggers to get temporary relief.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Is the word "obligation" referring to a contractual obligation or is it in relation to an obligation in general having regard to the purpose of the contract?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Let us deal with a contract dealing with a wedding dinner in a hotel.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The bride and groom’s obligation would be a payment obligation in which it may not be affected by a COVID-19 event as they would have set aside money for their wedding.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Read literally, they may not get relief if the obligation that they have is only a payment obligation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand the intention is to give relief to the bride and groom in such a parlous situation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the wording that is used in statute, I seek a clarification as to whether the obligation referred to in the clause is wider than the contractual obligation and should be referenced against the purpose of the contract that is objectively known to contracting parties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also would like to ask whether the clause is intended to apply on a mutual basis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Again, to illustrate, staying on the example, say, for example, if the hotel’s workers are all serving quarantine orders and, therefore, they are unable to proceed with the wedding dinner.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Can the hotel also take advantage of the clause?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If I am right, based on the definition of scheduled contracts in the Schedule, any company, not just SMEs, may use the measures in this Bill in relation to scheduled contracts, save for the finance-related contracts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If so, may I please ask why the hotels, which are naturally big boys, need to be protected under this Bill?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to clarify the meaning of this phrase.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I anticipate that Assessors appointed under the Act, once passed, will spend a lot of time on the meaning of this phrase.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In law, we have concepts, such as “causa causans” which is the immediate cause or the last link, or “causa sine qua non”, which is the cause that contributes to the loss even though it is not direct.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Or is the intent to provide relief even where there are more than one reason leading to a party being unable to perform an obligation in contract so long as the COVID-19 event is an important or significant reason.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is not clear is when this obligation is triggered.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under clause 5 of the Bill, it is stated that that the temporary relief kicks in upon satisfaction of three conditions, which include a notification under clause 5(c) to the other party.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This notification requirement is not specifically stated in the clause.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If so, would there not be situations where the owners or developers may act to call on bonds before being notified?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Now, this is not necessarily an unusual situation because the party that is unable to perform the obligation is not the party to the performance bond because that is between the employer and the bank.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It seems to me, however, if that happens, such acts may thwart the legislative intention behind the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may well be unconscionable conduct on the part of the owner or developer which ordinarily provides grounds to restrain payment under the bond.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would welcome clarification from the hon Minister on this point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, I go to the reference to arbitration under clause 5(3)(b) of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my personal view, arbitration seated in Singapore would be more consonant with the equivalent provision that deals with "Court" proceedings under clause 5(3)(a) of the Bill, which, taken together with the Interpretation Act, would mean "Courts of competent jurisdiction in Singapore".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, we should note that categories of scheduled contracts are not closed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also parties to domestic arbitration may have opted into the IAA regime, thereby, again possibly escaping this provision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My final point, Sir, is in relation to an area not specifically covered in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I appreciate that the two-witness rule in Singapore is put in to guard against fraud.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this day and age when we have Singpass for a whole host of digital services, this fraud issue could be contained to some extent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the meantime, I note that for this four-week period where generally all persons are to work from home, there is a carve-out in the Government measures that allows lawyers to provide drafting and execution of Will services as they constitute essential services.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Please allow me to declare my interest as Chairman of Sakae Holdings, President of the Singapore Manufacturing Federation (SMF), Vice-Chairman of the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) and Vice-President of the Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF).

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Since COVID-19 first became a major concern in Singapore, life has been riddled with much uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As the COVID-19 situation worsened over the last couple of months, people concerned with events, for example, have been brought on many different roller coasters.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: No, the event is not cancelled but will be limited to less than 40 people.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: A few days later, the event was reduced to 10 persons, with distancing measures and, a few days later, the event was postponed or moved to virtual means.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: But I must commend my fellow Singaporeans for being understanding and reasonable to bear with such uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is definitely not ideal for legal instruments not to be clear.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Over the last few weeks, Trade Association and Chambers (TACs), including the Singapore manufacturing Federation (SMF) have arranged for lawyers to give informative talks to our members on matters such as for "Fall, Merger and Frustration".

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It must have been frustrating for many, forgive the pun, that relief or threat of legal action depends on what is worded in the contract when the totally egalitarian COVID-19 virus does not discriminate between a super large organisation and a one-man show.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill now moves to bring a certain degree of clarity and uniformity in this unprecedented times is indeed welcomed by many in the business community.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is also opportune to add that by moving decisively and quickly in introducing this Bill, MinLaw is once again demonstrating its commendable foresight and dynamism.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is also creative thinking at its innovative best to use the law in such a manner to bring relief to the people and the community.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While we are mired in extraordinary times and it is imperative that we work and live together as a community.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is only if we go to the extra mile and practice consideration for one another that we have a higher chance that larger swaths of our societal fabric will be able to tide through this circumstances.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that many businesses know this concept inherently, but lack a framework or a former channel to practise some form of legal leniency and yet still, protect business interest.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I rise in support of the Bill and commend the Whole-of-Government approach to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Targeted protection from legal action is cited as one of the main objectives for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I believe this is crucial as the cash flow exposure for contractual obligations that they are now unable to fulfil weigh heavily on the minds of many business owners.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Under this Bill, five broad categories of contracts are identified and I stand by the decision to prioritise relief measures to address conflicts arising from these five areas.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: If I may I humbly suggest there should also be discussions on the expected payment schedule after the period of suspension, since it will be unlikely, for example, that a tenant will be able to pay six months of suspended rental immediately.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This is essential as this gives reassurance to the parties to whom payment is due, that there is a recourse for recovery of due fees in the future while not placing the pay in yet another difficult position.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: With this assurance, I hope parties are able to come to agreement in a cordial and amicable manner with the passage of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Once again, in light of the current situation, we are stronger if we seek to find solutions together.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In the event of future dispute after the Bill ceases effect, I would like to reiterate the points which is measured earlier in February in response to the reading of the Singapore convention on Mediation Bill.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Mediation should be an avenue considered by all parties to resolve any arising disputes.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: With mediation, the options for settlement are wider in scope than the monetary compensation available through arbitration or litigation, and parties have a chance to negotiate settlement options without prejudice to their legal rights and in a non-pressure cooker atmosphere.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: These concerns pertain more to the operational aspect of the Bill rather than the provisions of the Bill itself.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Once again, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I rise in support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has caused unprecedented disruption to all aspects of our lives and debilitated the economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Many businesses are struggling to cope with the on-going impact to their sales and operations, and many workers are struggling with income loss or even job loss.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I wish to speak on two specific aspects of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, relief for parties who are unable to perform their contractual obligations; and two, alternative measures for the holding of meetings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, I would like to speak on the proposed measures relating to the performance of contractual obligations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Many businesses are badly affected by the pandemic and have difficulty meeting their contractual obligations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I welcome the proposals to provide temporary relief from legal action for a party to a contract who is unable to perform its contractual obligations because of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Such contracts typically require the agency to pay liquidated damages if it fails to meet various obligations under the contract, such as ensuring that a specified number of security officers are present at the work site each day.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some agencies are unable to fulfil these requirements as their security officers are under quarantine orders or on leave of absence or are unable to come into Singapore as they are Malaysians.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I understand that there are cases of service buyers who insist on enforcing their contractual rights by claiming liquidated damages from the security agencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This imposes a heavy burden on these agencies, which are caught in a bind due to circumstances which are entirely beyond their control.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Furthermore, with the closure of most workplaces now, these agencies will most likely face the termination of a number of existing contracts, which will have a further adverse impact on their business and survivability.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Having said this, I would like to sound a cautionary note.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The proposed measures to provide relief under the Bill are fairly extensive and generous.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I believe all Singaporeans will recognise that they are a sincere attempt to ameliorate the tremendous pressures businesses face at this time.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, we must also be careful to ensure that they do not go too far, such that while one group is accorded relief, another group becomes adversely affected, or that the measures become subject to abuse.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, I wish to speak on the proposals relating to alternative methods to convene, hold or conduct meetings as required under any written law or legal instrument.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Trade unions registered in Singapore are required by their constitutions to conduct various types of meetings or conferences at specified times.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For example, many unions which are affiliated to the National Trades Union Congress, of which I am an Assistant Secretary-General, are required to hold a Delegates' Conference, which includes election of the union's Executive Committee, every four years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Prior to that, the unions may have to hold General Meetings at each of their branches, where branch leaders are elected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In addition, their constitutions require them to obtain the sanction of their delegates or members for large items of expenditure or to make changes to their constitution.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: NTUC has been receiving queries from several of our affiliated unions which are required to hold their Delegates' Conferences or members' meetings this year, and find that it may be difficult, if not impossible, to do so within the time frame mandated by their constitution.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I therefore welcome the proposal to allow the Minister to prescribe by Order alternative arrangements for the meeting.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Bill sets out some examples of possible alternative arrangements which may be prescribed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some of these are more relevant to entities such as companies or trusts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Where unions are concerned, some of these alternatives may not be workable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the same vein, besides Unions, there are associations, charities, co-operatives, religious organisations and clans which also have in their respective Constitutions and specified Regulations, process provisions to comply with – in the conduct of AGMs, voting and other meetings for approval of expenditure, leadership change as well as day-to-day operations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: A clearer articulation or a set of guidelines for the respective organisations to follow or make reference in these unusual times is welcomed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first was raised by Mr Louis Ng, the point about whether the Courts have oversight of why a party may choose not to consent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: No consent of the parties will be needed in such a situation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To the extent that there might be some prejudice to the accused person and the accused person does not consent, then in such a situation the Courts are unable to force the appearance of the witness by remote proceedings, and I hope that explains the situation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked about unions and the way in which unions might conduct their meetings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I believe I talked about this in my speech earlier as well as about the other types of different meetings that might take place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: No doubt, these particular considerations that might apply to one type of meetings or another will be taken into account when the Minister prescribes the alternative arrangements.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There were some points raised so let me provide quick clarifications.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, whether property owners who had acted quickly to pass on the property tax rebate before this Bill was introduced will be unduly penalised.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think it is very commendable that some property owners had indeed done so and I would like to assure everyone that these property owners will not be penalised for their earlier efforts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If these property owners had already passed on the rebate to each of their tenants in the form of monetary payment, rental reductions or an offset against current and future rental, consistent with the requirements in this Bill, the amount of rebate passed on earlier will satisfy the obligation imposed under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The second issue, the amount and the timeliness of property tax rebate passed on to the property owner's tenant.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is because property owners on instalment payment plans for their property tax will only receive the full benefit of the rebate by the end of the year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These two milestones therefore strike a balance between ensuring that property owners will not be required to pass on more than the rebate that they have received on hand and ensuring that they pass on the rebate in a timely manner to their tenants.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Third, whether master tenants are required to pass on the property tax rebate to their sub-tenants.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While we are cognisant that sub-tenants, namely the tenants of the property owners' tenants, are also impacted by the COVID-19 outbreak, the obligation under this Bill is on the property owner to only pass on the rebate to his own tenants.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It does not extend to requiring the property owner to pass the rebate to the sub-tenants or to require that the property owner ensures his own tenant passes the rebate to the latter's sub-tenant.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, we are very mindful that there is a whole range of commercial arrangements between tenants and sub-tenants.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not always a straightforward landlord and tenant relationship.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, there is no contractual between the property owner and the sub-tenant.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So it would be rather onerous to oblige the property owner to reach out all the way to the sub-tenants.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Nevertheless, we strongly urge and encourage all master tenants to pass on the savings from the rebate to their sub-tenants and to share the burden during this time of uncertainty and difficulty.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, the fine of $5,000 takes reference from the Property Tax Act, which sets a penalty for general offences at a fine of the same amount.
