speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I should remind everyone that the fine does not absolve a property owner of his obligation to pass on the property tax rebate to his tenants under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The property owner must still pass on the rebate fully in the prescribed manner and by the prescribed timelines.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On documentation required of property owners, property owners should ensure that they keep sufficient documentation to show clearly when the rebate was passed on and how much was passed on to their tenants.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the case where the property owner lets out a property to multiple tenants, then the owner should also keep documentation showing how he derived the amount of rebate to be passed on to each of his tenants.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Property owners can retain the relevant documentation in either soft copy or hard copy form so long as they remain available over a period of three years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We also strongly encourage property owners to ensure that their tenants acknowledge the property tax rebate received.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is to minimise potential disputes between the owner and the tenants on whether the rebate has been properly passed on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I tried to note down as many of the questions as I could.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I have missed out on any of them, it is not intentional.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zainal Sapari and Mr Patrick Tay asked if we could extend the protection that this Bill offers, to cleaning firms, security firms and others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same time, Members would have noted it gives me the power to add further categories of obligations and contracts beyond the five that are specified.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they can make a persuasive case, we will be prepared to add those categories, but always bearing in mind that this is not simply a case of – there is some problem and therefore we need to help people in their contracts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has got to go beyond that and be a matter of principle.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There should be unfairness in enforcing the contracts and we must find a fair way in resolving the issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Subject to that, my Second Reading opening speech made it very clear that we have a duty to help the people who have been affected by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We should not ask people, we should not require people to be held very strictly to the contracts if they have been affected by this massive event.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I can give the same answer, and the Member can take it up with us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we need to be careful about trading contracts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are many wide varieties of trading contracts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of them are international in nature and we ought to be careful about imposing our legal obligations on international parties, because that can also have a disproportionate impact on Singapore as a commercial hub.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we need to be careful about that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we are talking about trading contracts within Singapore, Mr Murali Pillai is a lawyer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it is a question of say, delivery of certain supply, and that supply is no longer available or supply has been affected by logistics, the contracts usually provide for relief in themselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if Mr Murali Pillai believes that over and above that, we can identify a class of contracts that can be circumscribed and be subject to relief, we will be happy to consider them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the item is for business, as I said in my speech, that will be protected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked about international arbitrations or arbitrations which are not local, and can there be a moratorium?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have been promoting Singapore as a cross-jurisdictional, international arbitration centre.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Two parties who are unconnected to Singapore often come to Singapore to arbitrate and I really do not think it is our business then to be saying automatically that there should be a moratorium.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a French man and a Chinese party have dealings with each other, and they have chosen Singapore because of its neutrality, and the law that applies is, let us say, a foreign law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Simply because they have chosen to come to Singapore, we should not impact on their arbitration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We should leave it to them to decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they have chosen Singapore law, then COVID-19 will become part of Singapore law if Parliament passes it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked, what about actions taken before this legislation comes into force?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, as I said earlier, that has got to unwound.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Other than that, if other actions have been taken, if properties have been possessed, it is difficult for us to go back and unwind retroactively.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But pending legal actions must be stayed if the categories of contracts are covered by the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about the scope of contracts that are covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He asked about wedding couples who want to cancel their bookings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It covers hotel bookings, it covers all goods and services relating to the event, and for those who have already cancelled, if the deposit has been forfeited, as I explained earlier, relief is available.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I have explained what sort of relief is possible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have also pointed out the need to balance between recovering the deposit immediately and the ability of the other party to pay, because everyone is suffering from COVID-19.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not mean that the event planner or the other contractual party who has taken the deposit can immediately pay back the deposit to everybody who is demanding immediate payment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there needs to be some justice, which is why we have gone via the route of Assessors to look at individual facts and decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about remedies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I spoke about it in my earlier speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, the event or the event planner or the hotel does not lose out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You do not lose out because your deposit is not lost.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If that is, for one reason or another, not possible or not suitable, if the contract has to be cancelled, then the question is how much to refund and what is a fair amount to be given back, and those are matters for the Assessors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just because you do not want to proceed with the event does not mean that you must get back 100%.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the event companies have spent some money, if they have done some work and so on, they need to be compensated for that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked about whether contracts for tours with travel agencies and air tickets will be covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Otherwise, alternate arrangements can be directed by the Assessors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Airlines have their own re-booking, refund and cancellation policies that are broadly similar internationally, and we should not intervene in those.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many airlines are currently sorting out those issues with their passengers as well as travel agents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Saktiandi asked about events that are slated for the later part of the year and whether the Bill could offer protection for such contracts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The answer is – his guess is as good as mine.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It depends on how long this situation lasts and how long the Bill is valid for; in the first place, as I have said, it will last for six months.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa expressed concern that the reliefs would trigger counter-claims because service providers could charge an upfront fee or price a risk of non-forfeiture in the fees charged.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, these points would not apply to this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because the parties are contracting with full knowledge – willing buyer, willing seller.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked whether relief under the Bill could apply on a mutual basis, for example, if a hotel was unable to proceed with the event because its workers are on Stay-at-Home Notice, and he asked why big companies ought to be covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the whole, the Bill helps the weaker party.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that does not mean always that the bigger party is at fault.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, if the hotel is unable to proceed because of COVID-19, is that the hotel's fault, and should we try and find some other alternate arrangement?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For any party to obtain relief, whether big or small, it would have to show that it was unable to perform the obligation and comply, meet the other requirements in the legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the hotel's workers are subject to Stay-at-Home Notices and it can show that it has got no other resources and cannot get any other workers, and if it complies with and fulfills the other conditions in the Bill, it will be covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan, Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Chong Kee Hiong all spoke about landlords, especially the smaller landlords who may require rent proceeds to service other obligations, such as mortgage payments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Saktiandi also spoke about landlords who are REITs, and Mr Chong Kee Hiong as well, and the eventual impact that non-payment of rent would have on retail investors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Bill does not alter the payment obligations of the tenants to the landlords.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The landlords can show the Assessors that the tenant, in fact, has the financial capacity to pay a part, if not all, of the rent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, how do we balance the interests of the landlords and the tenants?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong pointed out that the rate of return will be affected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I spoke at some length about rates of return.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think, at this point, the real question is not the rates of return but how do we protect the parties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even if we do not have this Bill, the rates of return are going to be impacted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How many tenants are going to be able to pay?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How many tenants are not going to be able to pay?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And when a tenant is not able to pay, you put him into bankruptcy, you put him into liquidation, are there a queue of tenants waiting to come in?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is it not going to affect the bottom line anyway?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, those are the realities of the current situation and the landlords are being helped in a significant number of ways.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I have said earlier, they are going to get 75% of their employee wage cost paid for in April.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are going to get Jobs Support Scheme (JSS) paid for their employees following that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are going to get the whole series of other benefits.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MAS has also worked with the financial institutions to provide for credit flow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Other issues that they may have in terms of people not paying rent and having a knock-on effect on their credit position, these are issues that I am sure MAS will be able to talk to them about and then talk to the banks about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We cannot prevent banks from exercising their rights, but I think, overall in Singapore, everyone can take a sensible approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Essentially, the relief is provided for tenants who are not going to be able to pay anyway.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, all these consequences that one sets out – oh, you know, this is going to impact on the rate of return, it is going to impact on the cash flow of the landlords and so on – but we are dealing with tenants who are not going to pay you, who are not able to pay you.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, you already have security deposits for a few months.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, your cash flow would not be affected for a few months.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I have indicated the Assessors will be given guidance that, in the first place, in general, they will say for three months, the tenant can suspend payment, if the tenant seeks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Assessor can give a longer period or shorter period but the general guidance will be three months.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong also made a good point about – and others, too – you know, supposing they get a six-month rental holiday, even if we set off two, three months, there will be some months of rental accrued and, at the end of that period, it will be a substantial amount.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Well, Mr Louis Ng had a suggestion for that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He asked why do we not be like the Germans?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Give an additional two years for them to pay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think the landlords would want that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same time, would it mean because some will not be able to pay, therefore, we should not even give them relief now?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That would effectively be an argument to say we should not intervene; we should let whoever is going to go bust, go bust, and that would inflict a lot of damage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The proposal we have, there is no perfect solution simply because the situation is very economically dire.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a question of how do you share out that pain?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we have a perfect solution where everyone can walk away with their contractual rights, of course, we would do that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, do we say some tenants will not be able to pay at the end of six months and, therefore, we should do nothing now?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, therefore, let a lot of other businesses which can pay go bust?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What will the REITs and the landlords be left with in such a situation eventually?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I would say to the bigger players, look, you are getting the benefits from the Government packages.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Play your part and help share some of the pain, too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It cannot simply be that you get all the benefits on one side and, on the other side, you only look at it in terms of your contractual rights.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This Bill is one part of, as I have said, the three aspects, the packages put up by the Deputy Prime Minister, the initiatives by MAS.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I understand the points that Mr Chong makes and some of the others make, and I know that some of it is with a genuine concern for tenants.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, really, we are on the same side seeing how we can help the tenants.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And is that best done by extending the payment period by two years and giving them a longer period to pay?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng had a couple of points which would have meant substantive intervention or substantive alteration of the rights.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One is to extend the period for payment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The other is even more radical – why do we not automatically reduce the rental?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I want to be very careful about it because, as Mr Chong Kee Hiong and others have pointed out, there are also landlords who are small businesses themselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They may have one small building with some tenants.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you tell them that the rent is going to be reduced automatically by a certain percentage, will they survive and is it fair to them?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are all issues that require much more careful deliberation by Ministries, beyond MinLaw.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It requires an economic analysis; it requires an assessment of how the situation plays out over the next few months.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Meanwhile, if the Bill passes, we apply a tourniquet, we hold the ring, we give people time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It also gives the time for the Government to assess the situation as it proceeds, do a deeper economic analysis to see whether any other interventions are justified.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have got to be very careful talking about these interventions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we say we are studying intervening in order to reduce the payments that tenants make, then you can be sure a lot of tenants, even those who can pay, will not pay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will say "Let us wait for what the Government is coming up with".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we say we are not going to deal with this, then a lot of landlords, who might have been willing to accommodate a better arrangement with their tenants, will say "Well, since the Government is not going to come in and do anything, therefore, we do not need to come in and help".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I think Ministers standing at this box need to be very careful in answering these questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can be sure that the economic agencies are actively looking at the situation and looking to see how best to handle it as we go forward, and they will take into account all the feedback that has been given.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr de Souza asked whether the Assessor can determine that the security deposit may be used to offset rental arrears.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not in every case that the Assessor will have to even decide, review after two to three months.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will depend on the circumstances and, really, if the parties can work it out themselves more sensibly, then it does not even have to go to the Assessor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked a related point whether putting in this Bill will give struggling tenants a false sense of hope that they may not need to pay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I expect that tenants, our commercial people, are quite savvy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am quite sure they will try and understand what the obligations are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in any event, MinLaw will put it out in very simple terms as much as possible and push it out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think even if the tenant is under such a misconception, I am sure the landlord will correct those misconceptions pretty soon.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked if the landlord will be prohibited from imposing interest on late penalty fees for rent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also spoke about this with respect to bank loans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are outside the scope of this Bill but Members will know that the MAS initiatives cover quite some aspects of what he has mentioned.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked if the Government will be putting in place further mechanisms to monitor the situation of smaller businesses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa also called for economic agencies to help companies cope with their payment obligations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Saktiandi asked whether the inability of businesses to fulfill contractual obligations would count against their credit ratings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These questions all raised broader policy questions beyond the ambit of this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can tell Members that the economic agencies are monitoring the economy very closely.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Jessica Tan spoke about construction contracts, how delay in construction contracts will impact individuals or businesses for whom the works have been committed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan also said that he has residents who cannot shift out of their tenanted residential homes because the contractors are not able to complete renovations due to the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Well, you can look at the Minister for Health.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has imposed the restrictions and there is nothing any of us can do about it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has actually made it into a criminal offence if you breach those regulations – Part 7 of this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is outside the scope of this Bill except to the extent that anyone wants to claim liquidated damages against the contractor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, what happens to all these people who are in temporary arrangements?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think everything has got to extend by a certain period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However long the Minister of Health tells you that you cannot move, you are stuck.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that in turn depends on health assessments which obviously must override all other considerations because if we are not careful there can be a substantial spread.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In those situations, the law outside of this Bill provides for certain types of reliefs, Mr Lim knows.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the rest of the works can be carried out later.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For those whose flats are undergoing transactions, sale purchase, the buyer and seller will have to discuss new dates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will seek to appoint a sufficient number of Assessors to ensure that the process is as quick as possible, as efficient as possible, and my Ministry will also be looking at implementing a quick and simple online process of making an application, sending documents, receiving determinations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hearings may also be held via video-conference where that is viable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa suggested giving Assessors powers to direct a process to restructure loans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That will be outside the scope and ambit of this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Assessors do not have that power and the primary purpose here is to suspend obligations for a period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lim asked what is to be done if there is clear prejudice shown by an Assessor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How would MinLaw ensure that the Assessor would always be impartial?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The process will have to comply with the rules of natural justice and judicial review remedies will be available, when there is breach of natural justice or corruption, for example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Douglas Foo asked if Assessors would be covered by indemnity insurance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Assessors will not be acting in their professional capacity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Bill provides that they will have no liability with respect to anything done in good faith, so there is protection.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali asked and sought clarification on the phrase "unable to perform an obligation", in relation to event contracts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is meant to cover the performance of obligations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The intention is to look at whether a party can perform a contract.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the situation that Mr Murali pointed out, the couple have as much obligation to accept the goods and services as an obligation to pay the price for it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the contract is to have a wedding banquet of a photography services, but they have become unable to accept the services because of the new measures, they are unable to perform.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali also sought clarification on the phrase "inability to a material extent caused by a COVID-19 event." The Bill is intended to cover situations where COVID-19 has meaningfully caused the inability to perform.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali also sought to clarify whether a contractor who intends to seek relief under clause 6, which prevents the other party from calling on a performance bond, has to serve notice on the other party.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the notification for relief is not served expeditiously, the other party may call on the performance bond.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A balance has to be struck between providing relief to the contract and certainty to the beneficiary in the event of default.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The paying bank also needs to know whether to honour the payment of the performance bond.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali recommended that MinLaw look at digitising wills, should the circuit breaker restrictions extend beyond four weeks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As we explained during the Committee of Supply or COS speech this year, we are reviewing the probate and administration regime and we will consider his suggestions as part of that review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Saktiandi asked what the Government is doing to ensure that the reliefs given to employers are reaching employees – whether in terms of helping them keep their jobs or upgrading their skills.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are outside the scope of this Bill and they were dealt with by the Deputy Prime Minister yesterday and today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Jessica Tan said that Assessors will review the moratorium after three months.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We left it out because pretty much everyone who takes or buys a vehicle on hire-purchase may be able to say that they need it for their work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They need it to travel to their workplace or they need it as an essential part of their work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that was not the intention of the clause.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The clause is, really to say that the vehicle is part of your goods and trade, like a van that is used to ferry people, cars used to ferry people in private hire business.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we will look at what he has said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, it is not a closed category and we can consider whether some refinements are possible in there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Douglas Foo, I think I have covered his point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I have covered the points that at least I wanted to cover.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, if Members have any supplementary questions, please return to your seat.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: It will make it easier for me to spot you.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I just wish to clarify that I did not raise in my speech the issue about landlords' dilemma.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And he mentioned the example of two parties outside Singapore having arbitration in Singapore and I completely understand where he is coming from.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The focus of my question, however, is to deal with situations where the subject matter is dealt with in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: You could have, for example, an international party against a Singapore company.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: That is also considered an international arbitration under the definition under the IAA so I wonder why in those circumstances, perhaps, the reference to arbitration being seated in Singapore could offer some kind of some kind of practical solution to companies who would also want to seek temporary relief under this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As to my setting out what he might have said in responding to things that he may not have said, I am entirely happy to accept that he may not have said it and I may have mistakenly ascribed to him what someone else has said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On arbitration, I understand the point that Mr Murali makes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Shanmugam, please proceed with the birthday celebration.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It could not be proceeded with – that was the issue.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The man approached the event organiser or the space provider to seek a refund or a postponement.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The event was intended to be held on 4 April.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The response was the agreement says it can only be postponed if the notice is given 30 days in advance.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Another case that was highlighted to us involved a couple who had engaged an event planner for their wedding.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The wedding banquet was meant for more than 500 guests and supposed to be held in June of this year.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When the couple approached the event planner, the event planner told them the event could not be postponed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The planner also told them obligations would be fulfilled even if the wedding did not take place on the date specified in the contract.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the positions adopted by the event space provider, event planner, I think are neither helpful nor reasonable.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But there are always two sides to every story.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A group of bridal studios wrote a joint letter to me, to highlight the challenges they are facing, with unreasonable couples.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The letter stated that couples had approached them “aggressively”, asking for a full refund of their packages.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They talked about the cash flow problems they are facing in the current climate.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They also pointed out why it was unfair to provide a full refund.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Their studios had provided services to the couples for up to a year before the wedding date and they had collected staggered payments along the way.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, these studios said they would be “very glad” to work out a postponement for the couples with no penalties imposed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Bill does not mandate that deposits be refunded immediately.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These decisions can be made by the Assessor if the parties cannot agree.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Assessors will make determinations that seek to provide a just and equitable outcome, looking at all the facts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The fourth category are hire-purchase agreements or conditional sales agreements.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These are agreements where the goods hired or conditionally sold under the agreement are: (a)	a plant, machinery or fixed asset used for manufacturing, production, or other business purposes; or (b)	commercial vehicles.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Over the course of the past week, we have received letters, petitions from a variety of people, including tour bus owners and drivers.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One letter we received stated that some excursion buses had been repossessed by financial companies.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Repossession basically means immediate termination from jobs for those who have lost their vehicles.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, many families’ lives, well-being is at stake, where the driver or owner of the bus is the sole breadwinner.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the aim of the Bill is to help them retain their business and their vehicles, where it makes sense to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The drivers, owners will be assisted by the measures introduced in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If they are commercial vehicles, they cannot be re-possessed during the prescribed period, if relief is sought and relief is given.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The fifth and final category are certain types of secured loan facilities given to SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These SMEs are defined as entities where the turnover of the group does not exceed $100 million in the latest financial year.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If such an SME is unable to repay its instalments to the financial institution due to a COVID-19 event, then some actions cannot be taken against it.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, security that it has given over real property or immovable property located in Singapore – you cannot enforce against that.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And there can be no enforcement of security against movable property if that movable property is a plant, machinery or fixed asset located in Singapore and used for manufacturing, production or other business purposes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have repeatedly emphasised – this is a crucial period, requires understanding from everyone.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some compromise and sacrifice is necessary from all sides to see us through this crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our approach is, we strongly encourage parties to try and come to a common understanding.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If resolution is not possible, the Bill provides for disputes to be settled by Assessors, who will be appointed by my Ministry.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The determinations made by Assessors – there will be no appeal.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The parties will not be allowed to have lawyers when going before Assessors.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And going before the Assessors is also free, no fees.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the Bill, we have designed the mechanism to provide for a quick, inexpensive and effective practical solution.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Subsidiary legislation will set out the procedure and practice for these proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They will try and hold hearings as quickly as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After submission of all relevant documents, there will be a guidance that they should hear these matters quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It also depends on the number of appeals they are faced up with and whether it is a complex dispute, requiring more documents.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are working hard to ensure that the necessary infrastructure is in place to facilitate this process.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The increase in the threshold means that more individuals can participate in the scheme to avoid bankruptcy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we are extending the minimum number of days that must elapse from the service of a statutory demand.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Which means, you have got to serve a notice and wait for six months.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the person must owe you at least $100,000 before you can proceed for bankruptcy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Likewise, we are going to deal with debts that companies owe for insolvency purposes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Bill will also provide a defence to an offence under section 144 of the Bankruptcy Act for a bankrupt who incurs debt without expectation of being able to pay for it.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is in the context of debts that were incurred during the period for which temporary measures apply and a similar defence will be provided in relation to the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018, as well as the Companies Act.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The measures in this Bill are one part of the wider efforts to address the impacts of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will do all we can to alleviate the economic pain being felt.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We cannot take away the pain completely, but we can help Singaporeans meet their immediate needs and ensure that our economy, as a whole, receives some help.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time – and this is a message that we have consistently reiterated – this is not a crisis that the Government acting on its own can overcome.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The essence of this Bill reflects that spirit.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If everyone looked after their own narrow self interests, we will not come through this crisis well.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Bill, therefore, provides a framework to hold the strict enforcement of certain legal rights in abeyance for a period of time.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That buys time for landlords and tenants, banks and lenders, other contracting parties, to focus their minds on how to get through the crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But the law can only go so far.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is also up to each individual Singaporean to have a sensa of fairness.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We hope that the spirit of SGUnited will underpin the many conversations to be had between contracting parties on how to move forward from this.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we are unable to pull together as a society, to have this sense of fairness, I am afraid that even the most interventionist of laws would not ensure that we can recover well.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We decided in late March that an intervention of this type is going to be necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We set up a committee of private sector professionals and different Ministries.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We had to be careful because, as Members will note, the total value of the sector that is being dealt with is over $120 billion.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: With the help of the committee, we were able to both conceptualise the ideas and draft the legislation in nine days.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The work involved many agencies – MOF, MTI, MND, MAS, AGC.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Two private sector lawyers, Sushil Nair and Patrick Ang, recognised as amongst the leading experts in their field, worked with us to conceptualise the framework, almost full time over the course of nine days.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Others in the committee included Mr Lim Sim Seng from DBS; Ong Yew Huat, now non-Executive Director of UOB; Andrew Lim, Group CFO of Capitaland; Keith Magnus, co-Chairman, Asia and Senior Managing Director of Evercore; Mr Ganesh from Soilbuild; Mr Melvin Ang, Chairman of an entertainment company MM2 Asia; and the Attorney-General Mr Lucien Wong himself, supervised the drafting of the Bill, clause by clause, together with outstanding officers from AGC.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We were lucky to have the AG himself personally involved.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As some here will know, he is recognised as world-class and the best corporate lawyer in Singapore when he was in practice.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He gave us much valuable advice – what worked, what was doable, what was not doable.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And because of him and his AGC team, the private sector professionals, and the Government agencies coming together, we were able to bring this Bill to Parliament so quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We owe them a lot in helping us with this Bill, and the large numbers of Singaporeans, who I hope will be helped by this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have made it such that we can add on to it because almost inevitably, issues will arise, and we could not have foreseen all of them.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will come back to Parliament where necessary and deal with them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: After the conclusion of proceedings on the Supplementary Supply (FY 2020) Bill.
